fields.title: Seven Times a Day
fields.subtitle: Monks, Mystics and Missionaries
fields.description: Seventeen short chapters on how the church prayed from about AD 500 to 1500: Benedict's hours of prayer, the praying church of Ethiopia, the Church of the East in China, Columba's Iona, Gregory of Narek, Anselm, Bernard, Francis and Clare of Assisi, Thomas Aquinas, The Cloud of Unknowing, the monks of Mount Athos, Julian of Norwich, Catherine of Siena, Wycliffe, Hus and Thomas à Kempis.
fields.about_html:
This book covers a thousand years, from the fall of the old Roman world in the West to the eve of the Reformation. People sometimes picture those centuries as a dark and empty time, but for the life of prayer they were anything but empty. In monasteries and villages, on islands and mountains, in great cities and along the trade roads of Asia, believers kept praying and taught the next generation to pray. It is Volume 5 of A Cloud of Praying Witnesses, an Ochorus series that follows the people of God at prayer from the Old Testament to the church around the world today.

Its seventeen chapters move in four parts. With the monks and missionaries we keep Benedict's seven hours of prayer, find the ancient church of Ethiopia, follow the Church of the East to China and land on Iona with Columba. Then we seek God's face with Gregory of Narek, Anselm, Bernard, Francis and Clare; learn from teachers and mystics such as Thomas Aquinas, the monks of Mount Athos, Julian of Norwich and Catherine of Siena; and come back to the Word with Wycliffe, Hus and Thomas à Kempis.

Every chapter tells its story from the oldest sources, says plainly where legend takes over and when a famous prayer is not really by the person whose name it carries. It quotes the witnesses word for word from their books in the library where it can, and ends with three key insights, a word for today, a practice to try, a closing prayer and questions for reflection. Two appendices gather every insight by theme and every Scripture in Bible order. Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, which is dedicated to the public domain.

qa.question: What is Seven Times a Day about?
qa.answer: How Christians prayed through the thousand years from about AD 500 to 1500: seventeen short chapters on monks and missionaries, seekers of God's face, teachers and mystics, and the first reformers, from Benedict and the church of Ethiopia to Julian of Norwich, Jan Hus and Thomas à Kempis.

qa.question: What is A Cloud of Praying Witnesses?
qa.answer: A series of books on prayer through the whole story of the church, named for Hebrews 12:1. The first four volumes follow prayer in the Old Testament, the teaching of Jesus, the first church, and the martyrs and desert fathers. This fifth volume follows the monks, mystics and missionaries of the next thousand years, and later volumes follow the praying men and women of every century and every part of the world.

qa.question: Do I need to read the volumes in order?
qa.answer: No. Each volume stands on its own. Reading them in order follows the story from Abraham to today, but you can begin with any volume.

qa.question: Why is it called Seven Times a Day?
qa.answer: The title comes from Psalm 119:164, "I praise you seven times every day", the verse Benedict used in his Rule for the hours of prayer that monks kept through the day. The book asks what that rhythm can teach ordinary believers today.

qa.question: Can I read it with a small group?
qa.answer: Yes. One chapter a day takes seventeen days on your own, and with a group one or two chapters a week works well. The questions at the end of every chapter are written to start a conversation.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every Scripture is quoted from the Open Word Bible (OWB), Balanced edition, a new translation from the Hebrew and Greek that is dedicated to the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: Where We Are in the Story
fields.body_html:
“Each generation will praise your works to the one after it and announce your mighty acts.” (Psalm 145:4)

This book covers a thousand years.

When it opens, around the year 500, the old Roman Empire in the West has fallen apart. Rome has been captured more than once. Roads are no longer safe, cities are shrinking, and many people fear for the future. When it closes, around the year 1500, the printing press has just been invented, ships are sailing to lands Europe did not know, and the church in the West is about to be shaken by the Reformation.

In between lie the centuries we often call the Middle Ages. People sometimes imagine them as a dark and empty time. For the life of prayer, they were anything but empty. In monasteries and villages, on islands and mountains, in great cities and on long trade roads, men and women kept praying, and taught the next generation to pray. As the psalm says, “each generation will praise your works to the one after it.”

Where we are in the series

This is the fifth volume of A Cloud of Praying Witnesses, a series that follows the people of God at prayer through the whole story of the church. The name comes from Hebrews 12:1, which pictures all the faithful who went before us as “so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us.”

Volume 1 listened to the prayers of the Old Testament, and Volume 2 sat with Jesus, the Teacher of Prayer. Volume 3 followed the apostles and the first church. Volume 4, Faithful unto Death, followed the martyrs who prayed in prison and at the stake, and the mothers and fathers who went out into the desert to pray.

This volume picks up their story. Many of its witnesses were the heirs of those desert monks. They lived in communities, kept set hours of prayer, copied the Scriptures by hand and carried the faith to new peoples.

The world of these witnesses

In these thousand years the church spread far beyond the Roman world, and it did not look the same everywhere.

In the East, the Christian empire based in Constantinople lasted until 1453, and its churches prayed in Greek. Further east, the Church of the East prayed in Syriac, from Persia to India and as far as China. In Africa, the ancient church of Ethiopia kept its own language, its own long fasts and its own songs. The Armenians, who count themselves the first nation to take Christ as its faith, prayed in Armenian. In the West, the church prayed in Latin, and its monks carried the gospel to Ireland, Britain and the peoples of northern Europe.

It was not an easy time. From the 600s, Islam spread across the Middle East and North Africa, and many old Christian lands came under new rulers. In 1054 the churches of East and West, which had been drifting apart for centuries, broke fellowship with each other. Wars were fought in the name of Christ that we cannot read about without sorrow. In the 1300s a terrible plague, the Black Death, killed perhaps a third of the people of Europe. And at times the church itself was rich, proud and divided, in need of renewal.

Through all of it, God kept a praying people. Most of the people in this book were not powerful. They were monks and nuns, teachers and preachers, a hermit in a small room in Norwich and a young woman in Siena. Many of them could not have imagined that their prayers would still be read hundreds of years later.

These witnesses come from Orthodox, Oriental, Catholic and early Protestant traditions, and some of their practices are still loved by some Christians and questioned by others. Where that is so, we will describe what they did simply and gently, and listen for what every believer can learn from them about prayer.

What we will see

This volume has seventeen chapters, in four movements:

  • Monks and missionaries (chapters 1 to 4). Benedict teaches his monks to stop and pray seven times a day. We find the praying church of Ethiopia, follow the Church of the East along the Silk Road to China, and land on the island of Iona with Columba, where every ordinary task became a reason to pray.
  • Seeking God’s face (chapters 5 to 9). Gregory of Narek cries to God from the depths of his heart in Armenia. Anselm asks God to teach him to seek Him. Bernard of Clairvaux learns that we love because God first loved us. Francis of Assisi calls all creation to praise, and Clare gazes on Christ until she begins to reflect Him.
  • Teachers and mystics (chapters 10 to 14). Thomas Aquinas prays before he studies. An unknown English writer teaches a simple reaching for God in The Cloud of Unknowing. The monks of Mount Athos wait in stillness before God. Julian of Norwich hears that “all shall be well,” and Catherine of Siena gives God no rest in prayer for His church.
  • Back to the Word (chapters 15 to 17). John Wycliffe and his followers put the Bible into English so ordinary people could pray it. Jan Hus prays for those who burn him. And Thomas à Kempis teaches a quiet heart to say to God, “Speak, for Your servant is listening.”

How each chapter works

Every chapter in this series has the same shape:

  • A key verse opens the chapter, the Scripture it rests on.
  • A story sets the scene.
  • The teaching looks at what the story shows us about prayer.
  • Voices from the past quote men and women of prayer, often the witnesses themselves, word for word from their own books in the Ochorus library.
  • Three key insights sum up what the chapter teaches.
  • For us today brings the lesson into ordinary life, wherever in the world you live.
  • Try this gives one simple practice for the coming week.
  • A closing prayer and Questions for reflection help you respond, alone or with others.
  • Read more on Ochorus points you to classic books where you can go deeper.

At the end of the book, two appendices gather all the key insights by theme and list every Scripture quoted, in Bible order, with the chapters where it appears.

A word about these stories

The stories in this book come from old sources: rules for monks, letters, chronicles, an inscription carved in stone, and the lives that friends and followers wrote. Some of these were written by eyewitnesses. Others were written much later, by people who loved these saints and sometimes added wonders to their stories. In each chapter we tell you where the story comes from, and when a detail is only a tradition, we say so. We also say so when a famous prayer was not really written by the person whose name it carries.

How to read this book

One chapter a day will carry you through the book in seventeen days. With a small group, one or two chapters a week works well.

The people in this book lived in a world very different from ours. Most had no Bible of their own, and many could not read. They had no clocks in their pockets, yet they kept hours of prayer. They had no easy way to travel, yet they carried the gospel across deserts, seas and mountains. Listen to them. They have much to teach a busy, hurried world about making room for God.

fields.title: Ora et Labora: Pray and Work
fields.body_html:
“I praise You seven times every day because Your rulings are righteous.” (Psalm 119:164)

Around the year 500, a young man left Rome behind. His name was Benedict. He came from Nursia, a town in the hills of central Italy, and had been sent to Rome to study. A Gothic king now ruled Italy, but Rome was still a city of schools and pleasures, and Benedict saw many students around him falling into careless and sinful lives. So, as his story was later told, he gave up his books and left his father’s house and wealth, “with a resolute mind only to serve God.”

He went about forty miles east into the hills, to a wild place called Subiaco, where a stream spread out into a lake. There he lived alone in a narrow cave for three years. Only one person knew he was there: a monk named Romanus from a monastery nearby, who saved part of his own bread for him. There was no path down the rock, so Romanus let the loaf down on a long rope with a little bell tied to it. When Benedict heard the bell, he came out to take his bread.

In time people found him, and many came to learn from him. One day a poor Goth, from the very people who now ruled Italy, came to join them. Benedict set him to clearing thorns beside the lake with a long-handled iron blade. The iron head flew off and sank into the deep water. Frightened, the man confessed what had happened. Benedict put the handle into the water, and, the story says, the iron rose and fitted itself onto the handle again. Benedict gave the tool back to him with these words: “Behold here is thy bill again, work on, and be sad no more.” (A “bill” was a farm tool for cutting brush.)

Later Benedict moved south to a high mountain above the town of Cassino, where country people still worshiped the old god Apollo. He pulled down the idol and built places of prayer there. On Monte Cassino he lived the rest of his life, and there he wrote a short Rule for his monks.

When he was dying, he asked his monks to carry him into the chapel. There, held up by his brothers’ arms, he stood with his own hands lifted to heaven, and as he prayed, he died.

Who told his story

The dates usually given for Benedict’s life, about 480 to about 547, are traditional and not certain. Almost everything we know about him comes from the Dialogues of Gregory the Great. Gregory, a monk who became bishop of Rome in 590, wrote about Benedict around 593, some fifty years after Benedict’s death. Gregory says he learned these stories from four of Benedict’s own disciples. He tells many wonders, as writers of saints’ lives did in his day, and we have told them as he does. But Gregory also says that the best picture of Benedict is in the Rule he wrote, because “the holy man could not otherwise teach, than himself lived.”

The Rule is a small book of seventy-three short chapters, drawing on older rules and on the teachers of the desert. In Volume 4, chapter 11, we saw that he told his monks to read John Cassian, and to begin each hour of prayer with Psalm 70:1: “God, come and rescue me! LORD, be quick to help me!” His gift was to gather that wisdom into a simple and balanced way of life. Gregory praised the Rule as “excellent for discretion,” that is, wise and moderate. Benedict himself called it a “least rule written for a beginning.”

Communities following the Rule spread across Western Europe. Catholic and Anglican monks and nuns still live by it today, and many other Christians have learned from it.

Seven times a day

Benedict built the day around prayer, taking his pattern from our verse. In an old English translation of his Rule (chapter 16), he writes: “As the Prophet saith: ‘Seven times a day I have given praise to Thee.’” So his monks met seven times between dawn and night, at the hours called Lauds (dawn), Prime, Terce, Sext and None (the first, third, sixth and ninth hours of the day), Vespers (evening) and Compline (before sleep). And because the same psalm says, “In the middle of the night I get up to thank You for Your righteous rulings” (Psalm 119:62), they also rose in the night to pray. Between them, these services covered all one hundred and fifty psalms every week.

Augustine had already explained what the number seven means in the Bible:

“Again, ‘Seven times a day will I praise Thee,’ which elsewhere is expressed thus, ‘I will bless the Lord at all times.’ And many such instances are found in the divine authorities, in which the number seven is, as I said, commonly used to express the whole, or the completeness of anything.”

Augustine of Hippo, The City of God

Seven times a day means the whole day. The hours were not meant to wall prayer into seven boxes, but to keep turning the whole day back toward God.

Benedict called this common prayer “the Work of God.” When the signal for prayer sounded, he wrote, each monk should leave “whatever he hath in his hands” and hurry to the chapel, and “let nothing be preferred to the Work of God” (chapter 43). When we sing the psalms, we should stand before God “that our mind may be in harmony with our voice” (chapter 19). And he reminded his monks that God does not hear us for our many words, so “prayer ought to be short and pure” (chapter 20).

Pray and work

Benedict’s way is often summed up in two Latin words, ora et labora, “pray and work.” The phrase is a good summary, but it is not in the Rule. It came into use later.

What the Rule does say is this: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul” (chapter 48). So the monks’ day was shared between prayer, reading the Scriptures and the work of their hands. Work was not the enemy of prayer. Benedict told the monk in charge of supplies to treat every pot and tool of the monastery “as if they were sacred vessels of the altar” (chapter 31). And he told his monks to welcome every guest as Christ Himself, because Jesus said, “when I was a stranger, you took Me into your home” (Matthew 25:35).

Gregory also wrote a book for church leaders, The Book of Pastoral Rule. In it he warned against two opposite dangers:

“The ruler should not relax his care for the things that are within in his occupation among the things that are without, nor neglect to provide for the things that are without in his solicitude for the things that are within; lest either, given up to the things that are without, he fall away from his inmost concerns, or, occupied only with the things that are within bestow not on his neighbours outside himself what he owes them.”

Gregory the Great, The Book of Pastoral Rule

“The things that are within” means our life with God; “the things that are without” means our work and our care for others. Benedict wanted both, held together by prayer.

Three key insights

  1. Praise offered seven times a day teaches us that the whole day belongs to God. Benedict’s monks did not wait until they felt like praying. The bell called them, again and again, and slowly their whole day was shaped by praise.
  2. Ordinary work, done for God, becomes part of our worship. The Goth’s lost blade and the pots of the kitchen mattered to Benedict. He told the man to “work on, and be sad no more.” No task is too humble to offer to God.
  3. Praying the Psalms together teaches us to pray with the whole church. The monks did not make up new words each hour. They prayed the Psalms, week after week, until God’s own words became their words.

For us today

A farmer in Malawi, a nurse in Manila or a mother of small children in São Paulo may hardly have one quiet hour, and certainly not seven. But Benedict’s lesson is not about a number. It is about rhythm. Daniel prayed “three times a day” (Daniel 6:10). The psalmist prayed “at evening, at morning and at noon” (Psalm 55:17). Any believer can mark the day with a few fixed moments.

Benedict also speaks to those who think their work is too humble to matter to God. Cleaning, selling in the market, cooking for a family: all of it can be done “as for the Lord and not for people” (Colossians 3:23).

And his world was full of war and disorder, as many believers’ worlds are today, in lands where governments are weak. Benedict did not wait for better times. He built a small community of steady prayer and honest work.

Try this

This week, try a simple rule of your own.

  • Choose your hours. Pick three or four fixed times each day, such as waking, noon, evening and bedtime. When the time comes, stop for one minute and pray.
  • Pray a psalm a day. Read one psalm slowly each morning, and let its words become your prayer.
  • Offer your work. Before you begin your work each day, say, “Lord, I do this for You.” When something goes wrong, remember Benedict’s words: work on, and be sad no more.

A closing prayer

Lord God, I praise You, because Your rulings are righteous. Thank You for Your servant Benedict, who taught his brothers to praise You seven times a day and to rise in the night to thank You. Teach me to turn my whole day toward You. When the time for prayer comes, help me to leave what is in my hands and come to You. Bless the work of my hands, and let it be done for You. Make my mind agree with my voice when I pray. And when my world is shaken, keep me steady in prayer and faithful in work, through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Benedict wanted “nothing” to be preferred to prayer. What most often comes before prayer in your day?
  • Which ordinary work in your life could you offer to God as worship?
  • What fixed times of prayer could you keep, even on your busiest days?

fields.title: Ethiopia Stretches Out Her Hands
fields.body_html:
“High officials will come out of Egypt; Cush will quickly lift its hands in prayer to God.” (Psalm 68:31)

The story begins almost two hundred years before this volume, on a ship in the Red Sea. A scholar named Meropius, from the city of Tyre, was traveling by sea to see distant lands. With him were two boys, his young relatives, named Frumentius and Aedesius. The ship stopped at a harbor to take on supplies. But a peace treaty between that land and the Romans had just been broken. The local people attacked the ship and killed everyone on board except the two boys. They spared them because they were so young, and took them to their king.

The king made Aedesius his cupbearer, the servant who poured his wine. Frumentius he made keeper of his records. Soon afterward the king died, leaving a widow and a little son. The queen begged the two young men to stay and help her govern until the boy was grown.

So Frumentius, a foreign captive, found himself helping to rule a kingdom. And he used his position for Christ. He looked for Christian merchants among the traders who came to that land, and urged them to find places where they could meet to worship. Socrates, a Greek church historian who later retold this account, says simply that “he built a house of prayer,” and taught some of the local people the faith.

When the young king came of age, the brothers asked to go home. Aedesius went back to Tyre. But Frumentius went to Alexandria in Egypt, to the bishop there, the great Athanasius whom we met in Volume 4. He begged him to send a bishop to the believers in that faraway land. Athanasius thought for a while, and then said that no one was more fit for the work than Frumentius himself. So Frumentius was made a bishop and sent back to the land of his captivity. Ethiopian Christians remember him to this day as Abba Salama, “Father of Peace.”

We have this story from Rufinus, a church historian who wrote around the year 400. He says he heard it from Aedesius himself, years later, when Aedesius had become a priest in Tyre.

An ancient African church

The kingdom was Aksum, in the highlands of what are now Ethiopia and Eritrea. Old writers sometimes called it “India,” because they used that name loosely for distant lands to the south and east. Its king in those years was Ezana. Athanasius himself, in a defense he wrote to the emperor Constantius, copied out a letter the emperor had sent “to Æzanes and Sazanes,” the princes of Aksum, demanding that they send Frumentius to Egypt to be examined by a bishop who opposed Athanasius. We have no sign that they obeyed. And coins from Ezana’s reign, which once carried the old pagan signs of the moon, began to carry the cross. By the middle of the 300s, the faith had reached the royal court.

But Ethiopian Christians trace their story back further still, to the court official whom Philip met on the road to Gaza, “a man from Ethiopia ... a high official in charge of all the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians” (Acts 8:27). His home was most likely the old kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan, rather than Aksum. Yet for many centuries African Christians have loved him as the firstfruits of their continent. Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching new believers in the 300s, connected him with our verse:

“He instructed the Eunuch, and baptized him, and so having sent into Ethiopia a herald of Christ, according as it is written, Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hand unto God, he was caught away by the Angel, and preached the Gospel in the cities in succession.”

Cyril of Jerusalem, The Catechetical Lectures

In the Hebrew of Psalm 68:31, the land is “Cush,” the country beyond the southern border of Egypt. The ancient Greek translation, from which the Bible in Ge’ez (the old language of Ethiopia) was first made, calls it “Ethiopia.” So Ethiopian believers have always read this verse as a promise about their own people, lifting their hands to God in prayer.

The years of this volume deepened that faith. In the late 400s, tradition says, nine monks came from lands of the Roman Empire. The church remembers them as the Nine Saints. They founded monasteries in the north, such as Debre Damo on its high flat-topped mountain, and are said to have helped translate the Scriptures into Ge’ez. In the 500s, tradition says, a church musician named Yared gave the church its chant, the music still sung in its worship. Later, when the rise of Islam cut Ethiopia off from much of the Christian world, the church held on in its mountains for centuries.

Around 1200, a king named Lalibela had eleven churches cut down into the solid rock of the mountains. Tradition says he wanted to make a new Jerusalem in Ethiopia for those who could not travel to the old one. Scholars still study how and when each was made, but they are still used for prayer every day.

How they prayed

Much about these early centuries is tradition. But some things about this church’s prayer are clear, and they have lasted.

First, it is a church of the Psalms. The Ge’ez Psalter, often called simply Dawit (“David”), contains the psalms together with songs from other parts of the Bible, such as the songs of Moses and of Hannah. In the traditional church schools, a child who has learned to read goes on to the Psalter, and many learn it by heart. Priests, monks and ordinary believers pray from it every day: “Deep in my heart I have kept Your word safe” (Psalm 119:11).

Second, it is a church of the hours. Like the other ancient churches, it keeps set times of prayer through the day and night. Around 1400 a learned monk named Giyorgis wrote a Book of Hours that became widely used in Ethiopian prayer.

Third, it is a church of fasting. Ethiopian Orthodox Christians keep many fast days each year: every Wednesday and Friday, a long fast of fifty-five days before Easter, and other seasons as well, about one hundred and eighty days for ordinary believers and more for priests and monks. On those days they eat no meat, milk or eggs, and often nothing at all until the afternoon. Fasting and prayer go together, as Jesus taught: “when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that no one but your Father, who is there in secret, will know that you are fasting” (Matthew 6:17-18).

Ethiopian believers also pray with their bodies. They take off their shoes before entering a church, because God told Moses, “Remove your sandals from your feet, because the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). They bow to the ground in prayer and stand for long hours in worship. Body and soul together lift their hands to God.

Three key insights

  1. God’s promise reached Africa long before many other lands heard the gospel. Psalm 68:31 looked ahead to the day when the peoples south of Egypt would pray to the true God. Ethiopia’s church is one of the oldest in the world, and it is African.
  2. God can use a captive to bring His light to a nation. Frumentius came to Aksum as a prisoner. He used the place God had put him to gather believers and build a house of prayer.
  3. Fasting together, as a whole church, teaches us that we need God more than food. For sixteen centuries Ethiopian believers, rich and poor alike, have kept the same fast days together. Going without food for a while makes room for prayer and reminds us how much we depend on God.

For us today

Some people think Christianity is a Western religion that reached Africa only recently. Ethiopia’s story says otherwise. African believers were praying the Psalms in their own language while much of northern Europe still worshiped other gods. If you are an African Christian, you belong to one of the oldest families of faith in the world.

The story also speaks to believers far from home: house workers in the Gulf, refugees in camps, students in foreign cities. Like Frumentius, you may feel powerless. But God can use you right where you are to gather others for prayer.

And Ethiopia’s fasting is a gentle challenge to those of us who eat whenever we like. Fasting is not a way to earn God’s favor. It is a way of humbling ourselves before Him and making room to pray.

Try this

This week, learn from the prayer of the Ethiopian church.

  • Lift your hands. When you pray this week, lift your hands, as our verse says, as a sign that you are reaching out to God.
  • Fast for one day. If your health allows, choose one day, perhaps Wednesday or Friday, and skip a meal or eat only simple food. Use the time you save to pray.
  • Pray for the church in Ethiopia and Eritrea. Ask God to bless believers there, and to strengthen those who suffer for their faith.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You promised that the peoples beyond Egypt would lift their hands in prayer to You, and You kept Your word. Thank You for the court official who believed and went home rejoicing, for Frumentius who built a house of prayer in a strange land, and for the many generations of Ethiopian believers who have fasted, sung the Psalms and kept the hours of prayer. Teach me to let go of what is seen and to hold on to You. Use me wherever You have placed me, and bless Your church in Africa and in every land, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Frumentius arrived in Aksum as a captive. How might God use the place where you are right now, even if you did not choose it?
  • Why do you think fasting and prayer have gone together for so long in the Ethiopian church?
  • What does it mean to you that one of the oldest churches in the world is in Africa?

fields.title: Prayer on the Silk Road
fields.body_html:
“From where the sun rises to where it sets, My name is great among the nations. In every place incense is offered to My name, and pure offerings, because My name is great among the nations, says the LORD of Armies.” (Malachi 1:11)

In the year 635, a group of travelers arrived at Chang’an, the capital of China under the Tang emperors and one of the largest cities in the world. Merchants arrived there by the Silk Road, the long chain of trade routes across the deserts and mountains of Central Asia. But these travelers were monks. Their leader was a man the Chinese called Alopen. They had come a very long way from the far west, and they carried books.

The emperor Taizong, a learned man, sent one of his chief ministers, Fang Xuanling, out to the west to welcome Alopen and bring him in. The monks’ books were taken to the imperial library to be translated into Chinese, and the emperor studied them in his own rooms. Three years later, in 638, he issued an order that the new teaching should be allowed to spread. He said, in an old English translation, that it was “beneficial to all creatures” and “advantageous to mankind.” He ordered a monastery to be built in the capital, served by twenty-one priests.

So the gospel of Jesus Christ came to China, more than six hundred years before the first Catholic missionaries arrived in the 1290s, and nearly twelve hundred years before the first Protestant missionaries of the 1800s.

We know this story because, almost a century and a half later, in 781, the Christians of Chang’an set up a tall stone tablet about nine feet high. At its top they carved a cross. Below it, in nearly two thousand Chinese characters, they told what they believed and how their church had come to China. Along the edges, in Syriac, the language of their worship, they carved the names of their bishop and of many priests. The stone describes Alopen’s journey in poetic words: “Observing the azure clouds, he bore the true sacred books; beholding the direction of the winds, he braved difficulties and dangers.”

Who they were

Alopen belonged to the Church of the East. Its home was in Mesopotamia and Persia, in what are now Iraq and Iran, and it prayed in Syriac, a language close to the Aramaic that Jesus spoke. While the churches of Rome and Constantinople grew within the Roman Empire, this church grew outside it, eastward. Its monks and merchants carried the faith along the trade routes to Central Asia, to India and, at last, to China. (Others called them “Nestorians,” after a bishop whose teaching they were thought to follow. Their descendants still worship today, in Iraq, Iran, India and beyond.)

In China they called their faith Jingjiao, “the luminous religion,” the religion of light. The stone gives a careful reason for the name: the true teaching is hard to name, “but as its meritorious operations are manifestly displayed, by accommodation it is named the Illustrious Religion.” John wrote of Jesus: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (John 1:5).

We should be honest about how much we do not know. The stone was written by a monk named Jingjing, called Adam in Syriac, and it praises the emperors warmly, as such stones did. It says that in one emperor’s day “every city was full of churches,” which was probably a large exaggeration. Some Christian writings from these years, found in the early 1900s in a sealed cave near Dunhuang in western China, borrowed so many Buddhist and Daoist words that scholars still debate how clearly they spoke of Christ. A list in one of them names about thirty-five books that had been translated into Chinese, including the Psalms. Almost all are lost.

How they prayed

The stone speaks of baptism, of the cross, and of “twenty-seven sacred books,” the New Testament. And it describes how the monks lived:

“As they strike the wood, the fame of their benevolence is diffused abroad; worshiping toward the east, they hasten on the way to life and glory.” The monks were called to prayer by striking a wooden board, as many Eastern monasteries still do. They faced east when they prayed, toward the rising sun, as a sign that they were looking for Christ’s return.

The stone goes on: “they do not keep slaves, but put noble and mean all on an equality.” And: “seven times a day they have worship and praise for the benefit of the living and the dead.” Far away in Italy, Benedict’s monks were keeping seven hours of prayer, as we saw in chapter 1. Here, at the other end of Asia, the same psalm was being prayed by monks who had never heard of him.

Their prayer led them to love. The stone tells of a priest named Yisi who gave away his wealth: “the naked came and were clothed; the sick were attended to and restored; the dead were buried in repose.”

What was lost

For two hundred years the church in China lived and prayed. Then, in 845, the emperor Wuzong turned against foreign religions. Buddhist monasteries were closed by the thousands, and Christian monks were also forced to leave their monasteries and return to ordinary life. Many think the Christians of Chang’an buried their stone at about this time to keep it safe. In 987 a monk who had just come back from China told Ibn al-Nadim, a writer in Baghdad, that the Christians there had almost all disappeared.

The faith came back under the Mongol emperors in the 1200s and 1300s, and then faded again. The stone lay forgotten in the earth for nearly eight hundred years, until it was dug up near Xi’an, as Chang’an is now called, in the 1620s. It stands today in a museum in that city.

Does that mean the prayers of those monks were wasted? E. M. Bounds, the American pastor, would answer no:

“Prayers are deathless. The lips that uttered them may be closed in death, the heart that felt them may have ceased to beat, but the prayers live before God, and God’s heart is set on them and prayers outlive the lives of those who uttered them; outlive a generation, outlive an age, outlive a world.”

E. M. Bounds, Purpose in Prayer

Malachi spoke these words to priests in Jerusalem who were offering God careless worship. God told them that His name would be great far beyond Israel, “from where the sun rises to where it sets.” In the Bible, incense is a picture of prayer: “Let my prayer stand before You like incense” (Psalm 141:2). In Revelation, the elders in heaven hold “gold bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of God’s holy people” (Revelation 5:8). The incense of those monks in Chang’an is in those bowls.

In the 1800s, Maria W. Stewart, an African American writer and speaker, prayed for the same promise:

“Bless thy churches throughout the whole world. Clothe thy ministers with salvation, and cause thy saints to shout for joy. Grant that the time may soon come that all may know thee, from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.”

Maria W. Stewart, Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart

Three key insights

  1. God’s name is great among the nations, and His people pray to Him in every place. Long before modern missions, believers were praising God in Syriac and Chinese across the whole of Asia. Malachi’s promise was already coming true.
  2. No prayer offered to God is lost, even when the church that prayed it is forgotten. The church in Tang China almost disappeared. But its prayers rose to God, and He keeps them.
  3. The church’s true strength is in prayer and love, not in the favor of the powerful. The church in Tang China rose with the emperors’ favor and fell when it was taken away. What lasts is faith rooted in ordinary believers who pray.

For us today

Today there are many millions of Christians in China. Most of them came to faith in the last hundred years, often through great suffering. They are the heirs of a much older story. The first believers in China knelt facing the sunrise thirteen centuries ago.

This chapter comforts believers where the church is small, watched or pushed aside: your prayers are not wasted. It also warns churches that lean on governments or wealthy friends. The faith that lasts lives in homes and hearts, in the language of the people.

And the church is bigger than our own tradition. While Benedict prayed in Italy and Ethiopian monks sang the Psalms in their mountains, monks of the Church of the East were praying the same psalms in Chang’an. From where the sun rises to where it sets, one family was praying.

Try this

This week, let your prayers travel along the Silk Road.

  • Face the sunrise. One morning this week, look toward the rising sun and pray Malachi 1:11 or Psalm 113:3: “From where the sun comes up to where it goes down, the name of the LORD is worthy of praise.”
  • Pray across Asia. Each day, pray for believers in one country along the old Silk Road: China, Mongolia, Iran, Iraq, the lands of Central Asia.
  • Pray for the Church of the East today. Many of its people in Iraq, Iran and Syria have suffered greatly. Ask God to strengthen and protect them.

A closing prayer

Lord of Armies, Your name is great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets. Thank You for Alopen and the monks who carried Your word across deserts and mountains to China, and prayed seven times a day far from home. Thank You that no prayer offered to You is lost. Let my prayer stand before You like incense. Strengthen Your church in China and in every land along the old roads of Asia. Make Your light shine in the darkness, and let all the earth know You, through Jesus Christ, the Light of the world. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • What surprises you most about the story of the church in Tang China?
  • Why do you think the church in China nearly disappeared after 845? What can churches today learn from that?
  • How does it encourage you that your prayers rise before God like incense and are kept by Him?

  • Maria W. Stewart, Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart, especially “Meditation VIII”

fields.title: The Prayers of Ordinary Days
fields.body_html:
“The LORD will guard you as you set out and as you return, from now on and for all time.” (Psalm 121:8)

It was a Saturday in early June, in the year 597, on the small island of Iona, off the west coast of Scotland. An old abbot named Columba, bent with age, walked slowly with his helper Diormit to the monastery’s barn. He went in and blessed it, and the two heaps of grain that lay inside. Then he gave thanks that his monks would have enough bread for the coming year, even if he had to leave them.

Diormit was troubled. Lately the old man kept speaking of leaving. Columba made him promise to keep a secret, and then told him: today was the Sabbath, the day of rest, and it would be his last day of work. That night, at midnight, as the Lord’s Day began, the Lord Jesus would call him home.

On the way back, Columba sat down by the road to rest. The old white horse that carried the milk pails from the cowshed came up to him and laid its head on his chest, as if it knew. Diormit tried to drive it away, but Columba stopped him, and blessed the horse before it turned away.

Then he climbed the small hill above the monastery. He lifted both his hands and blessed the place where he had lived and prayed for more than thirty years. He went back to his hut and sat down to his daily work: copying the book of Psalms by hand. He came to Psalm 34 and wrote the verse, “those who seek the LORD will never be without anything good” (Psalm 34:10). There he stopped, and said that his successor should write the rest.

He went to the evening service that began the Lord’s Day. Afterward he lay down on his bed, which was a bare stone slab, with a stone for a pillow, and spoke his last words for his monks, with only Diormit there to hear them: that they should “be at peace, and have unfeigned charity among yourselves.”

When the bell rang at midnight, he rose quickly and hurried to the church, ahead of all the others, and knelt in prayer before the altar. Diormit found him there in the dark and held his head. As the brothers came running in with lamps, the old man opened his eyes and looked around with a face full of joy. Diormit lifted Columba’s right hand, and he moved it a little to bless them. Then he died.

Who he was

We have this story from Adomnán, the ninth abbot of Iona, who wrote a Life of Columba about a hundred years later, around the year 700. Adomnán used older writings and the memories of old monks. He also tells many wonders, as writers of his day did.

Columba was born in Ireland around 521, into a powerful royal family in the north. Patrick, whose story we told in Volume 4, had already planted the faith in Ireland, and Columba grew up in its young monasteries, as a student, a monk and a founder of new communities. Then, Adomnán says, in the forty-second year of his age, “resolving to seek a foreign country for the love of Christ,” he sailed with twelve companions to Britain. (Adomnán dates his leaving by a battle fought two years before. Later Irish stories link his going to that battle and to a quarrel over a book, but they were told much later, and we cannot be sure of them.) The year was 563.

On Iona he built a simple monastery. From there he and his monks traveled to the Picts, the people of northern Scotland. Adomnán tells how Columba and a few brothers sang the evening hymns outside the fortress of King Brude, near today’s Inverness, even when pagan priests tried to silence them. In the next century, monks from Iona carried the gospel south into England.

Adomnán sums up Columba’s life in a few words: “He never could spend the space of even one hour without study, or prayer, or writing, or some other holy occupation.” Yet he was not a gloomy man. Adomnán says he was loved by all, “for a holy joy ever beaming on his face revealed the joy and gladness with which the Holy Spirit filled his inmost soul.”

Blessing ordinary things

Look again at Columba’s last day. He blessed a barn, a work horse and a small monastery, copied a psalm and went to church. These were ordinary things, and he brought each of them to God.

Adomnán gives other glimpses of this. A young man coming back from milking the cows stopped at Columba’s door with a pail of new milk on his back and asked him to bless it, “as he usually did.” Another day a brother asked him to bless a knife. Columba was busy writing, so he did not even turn from his book. He simply reached out his hand, with the pen still in it, and blessed the knife. Prayer was part of the work of the day, not separate from it.

This was the old way of God’s people. Moses told Israel to speak of God’s words “as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Paul wrote, “when you eat, when you drink, whatever you do, do everything for God’s glory” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Many people today love what are called “Celtic prayers,” short blessings for lighting the fire, milking the cow or setting out on a journey. A word of care is needed. Most of the famous ones come from the Carmina Gadelica, a collection made by Alexander Carmichael from the Gaelic-speaking people of the Scottish Highlands and Islands in the 1800s and published in 1900. They are beautiful, but they cannot be dated to Columba’s time, and Carmichael seems to have polished some of them. Still, they show how, many centuries after Columba, ordinary people in the same lands prayed over every task. A woman lighting her fire in the morning would pray, “God, kindle Thou in my heart within / A flame of love to my neighbour.” At night, covering the coals to keep them till morning, she would ask “the sacred Three / To save, / To shield, / To surround / The hearth, / The house, / The household.”

The same spirit is found in Psalm 121, a pilgrim’s song. The Lord guards our setting out and our return. D. L. Moody, the American preacher, said this about it:

“Some one calls that the traveler’s psalm. It is a beautiful psalm for those of us who are pilgrims through this world; and one with which we should be well acquainted. God can do what He has done before.”

D. L. Moody, The Way to God

Columba was such a pilgrim, a man who left his own country “for the love of Christ.”

Three key insights

  1. No part of an ordinary day is too small to bring to God in prayer. Columba blessed grain, milk, a knife and an old horse. God cares about our daily bread and our daily work, and He welcomes us to bring them to Him.
  2. The Lord who guards our going out and coming in is with us on every road. Columba left his homeland for Christ and never went back to live there. Psalm 121 promises that God watches over every journey, from the first step to the last.
  3. A blessing can be our last gift to those we love. Columba’s last words were a call to peace and love, and his last movement was a blessing. Daily prayer had shaped him, until blessing others was what he did by habit.

For us today

Most of us do not live in monasteries. We light stoves, catch buses, sell in markets, care for animals and children. A farmer in the Andes, a taxi driver in Lagos, a mother cooking on a gas ring in a crowded flat in Mumbai: each of them can bless the work of the day in a few words.

Columba’s story also speaks to people who travel. Millions of believers today leave home to find work, to study or to escape danger. Some never return. Psalm 121:8 is a promise for them: the Lord guards our setting out and our return.

And it reminds us to bless. Parents can bless their children before school, and friends can bless one another at the door. To bless is simply to ask God’s good upon someone, in Jesus’ name.

Try this

This week, bring the ordinary moments of your day to God.

  • Bless your first task. When you light the stove, make tea or start your work, pray, “God, kindle in my heart a flame of love to my neighbor.”
  • Bless your going out. At your door each morning, say Psalm 121:8: “The LORD will guard you as you set out and as you return.”
  • Bless your home at night. Before sleep, ask God to save, shield and surround your house and everyone in it.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You guard my setting out and my return, from now on and for all time. Thank You for Columba, who left his home for the love of Christ, who blessed the grain, the milk and the work of every day, and who died blessing his brothers. Teach me to bring every ordinary moment to You. Bless the work of my hands and the food on my table. Guard my family as we go out and come in. Kindle in my heart a flame of love for my neighbor, my friend and my enemy. And when my last day comes, let me be found at prayer, at peace and full of love, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Columba blessed a barn, a horse and a pail of milk. What ordinary things in your life could you bring to God in prayer?
  • Why do you think Columba’s last words were about peace and love?
  • Where do you most need to remember that the Lord guards your going out and your coming in?

fields.title: Out of the Depths
fields.body_html:
“From the deep waters I call to You, LORD. Lord, listen to me as I call! Turn Your ears toward my cry for mercy. LORD, if You kept count of every wrong, Lord, who could stand before You? But forgiveness is found with You, and so You are held in awe.” (Psalm 130:1-4)

On the southern shore of Lake Van, in the high mountain country of Armenia, there stood a monastery called Narek. Around the year 1002, an old monk there was finishing a book. His name was Grigor, and we know him as Gregory of Narek.

We do not know what his room looked like, or what time of day he wrote. We do know what he wrote. He wrote prayers: ninety-five of them, more than ten thousand lines in all. Almost every one of them carries the same heading, which is often put into English as “Speaking with God from the depths of the heart.”

That heading tells us what kind of book it is. It is not a book about God. It is a book spoken to God, from beginning to end. Gregory does not hide anything. He confesses his sins in great detail and spares himself nothing. He says he has wanted to be perfect, as Jesus taught, and has failed again and again. He calls himself the lowest of sinners, and he means it.

But that is not where his prayers end. Again and again, just when he seems about to sink, he turns to the mercy of God. He remembers that Christ came for sinners. He remembers baptism, the cross and the Lord’s table. He praises God’s kindness in long, rich lines, as if one word could never be enough. Out of the depths of shame, he rises to hope.

Gregory died soon after he finished the book, perhaps in 1003, though some scholars think a few years later. He was buried inside the monastery walls. The book outlived him by a thousand years. Armenians simply called it the Narek, after his monastery. They copied it by hand, kept it in their homes and read it to the sick. Scholars say that for many Armenian families it was the most treasured book after the Bible itself.

A church in the mountains

The Armenian people live in the mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. According to their tradition, in about the year 301 a missionary named Gregory the Illuminator brought King Tiridates III to faith in Christ, and the king made Christianity the faith of his kingdom. If that date is right, Armenia was the first nation in the world to do so, even before the Roman Empire.

About a hundred years later, a monk named Mesrop Mashtots made an alphabet for the Armenian language, so that the people could read the Bible in their own tongue. The Armenian Apostolic Church has kept its own worship, music and customs ever since. It is one of the ancient churches of the East, often called the Oriental Orthodox churches, along with the churches of Ethiopia and Egypt.

Gregory of Narek was born about 950 near Lake Van. His mother died when he was small. His father became a bishop, and Gregory was sent as a boy to the monastery of Narek, where his great-uncle was the teacher. He became a priest there in 977 and taught at its school for the rest of his life. He also wrote hymns that are still sung in Armenian churches.

The Armenian church honors him as a saint, and in 2015 the Catholic Church named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for all believers. The monastery of Narek no longer stands. It was abandoned after the terrible killing of Armenians in 1915 and later destroyed. But his prayers went wherever Armenians went.

How he prayed

As far as we know, there is no old public-domain English translation of Gregory’s book, so in this chapter we describe his prayers rather than quote them.

His prayers are long and honest. He does not ask God to look at his good works. He asks God to look at Christ. He knows the words of the tax collector, “God, be merciful to me, the sinner!” (Luke 18:13), and his whole book is that short prayer spread out over many pages.

Readers have often noticed something else. Gregory’s “I” is very wide. When he confesses, he seems to speak not only for himself but for every sinner who will ever pick up his book. He gives us words for feelings we could not name. That is one reason the Narek became a family prayer book. A grandmother who had never studied could open it and find her own heart on the page.

Long before Gregory, John Chrysostom gave the same advice about prayer from the heart:

“Out of deeps call upon God, for it is said, “Out of the depths have I cried to Thee, O Lord.” From beneath, out of the heart, draw forth a voice, make thy prayer a mystery.”

John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew

What the psalm teaches

Psalm 130 is one of the “songs of ascents.” Many think these were sung by God’s people as they walked up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. Older English Bibles begin it, “Out of the depths.” The “deep waters” are not the sea. They are the depths of a heart that knows it has done wrong.

Notice what the psalm says. If God kept a list of every wrong, no one could stand before Him. Not the priest, not the king, not the monk of Narek, not you or me. “But forgiveness is found with You.” That little word “but” is the turning point of the whole psalm, and of Gregory’s whole book.

Then comes a surprise: “and so You are held in awe.” We might expect the psalm to say that God’s forgiveness makes us relaxed, or careless. Instead it says that forgiveness makes us bow down in wonder. Someone who has been forgiven much does not treat God carelessly. He trembles with love.

The psalm then turns to waiting: “I long for the Lord more than night guards long for the morning” (Psalm 130:6). A guard on a city wall watches all night. He cannot make the sun rise. But he knows it will come. So we wait for God’s mercy, not because we have earned it, but because He has promised it.

Charles Spurgeon, the London preacher, knew that the deepest prayers often come from the lowest places:

“There is no cry so good as that which comes from the bottom of the mountains; no prayer half so hearty as that which comes up from the depths of the soul, through deep trials and afflictions.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Morning by Morning

In Volume 1 we went down with Jonah into the depths of the sea. Gregory takes us into another kind of depth: the hidden places of our own hearts. God hears from there too.

Three key insights

  1. Honest confession is the doorway to God’s mercy, not a wall against it. Gregory held nothing back from God, and his prayers always ended in hope. We do not need to hide our sins from God; He already sees them, and He waits to forgive.
  2. God forgives us so that we will hold Him in awe, not so that we will treat sin as a small thing. Psalm 130 says that forgiveness leads to wonder. The more we understand how much we have been forgiven, the more we love and honor the One who forgave us.
  3. The prayers of others can give us words when our own words fail. For a thousand years, Armenian believers prayed with Gregory’s words. The Psalms, and the prayers of faithful believers, can carry us when we do not know what to say.

For us today

Many of us carry things we have never said aloud to anyone. A man in Nairobi remembers what he did in his youth. A mother in Jakarta cannot forgive herself for words she spoke in anger. A pastor in Mexico City smiles on Sunday and feels empty inside. Gregory shows us that we can bring all of it to God. The depths are not too deep for Him to hear.

Gregory’s book also speaks to people who have suffered greatly. The Armenian people have known invasion, exile and killing. Many lost their homes and their land. Yet they carried this prayer book with them across the world. Believers in places of persecution today can do the same: they may lose buildings, but no one can take away the prayers in their hearts.

And Gregory reminds us that we do not need to be clever to pray. We need only to be honest.

Try this

This week, let Psalm 130 and Gregory of Narek teach you to pray from the depths.

  • Pray the psalm slowly. Read Psalm 130 aloud each day. Stop at the word “But” in verse 4, and thank God for His forgiveness.
  • Speak from the depths. Find a quiet place and tell God one thing you have never told anyone. Then read 1 John 1:9 and receive His promise.
  • Wait like a night guard. If you are waiting for God to answer a prayer, write down Psalm 130:6 and keep it where you will see it each morning.
  • Pray for the Armenian church. Ask God to bless Armenian believers in Armenia and around the world, and all Christians who have lost their homeland.

A closing prayer

Lord God, from the deep places of my heart I call to You. If You kept count of every wrong, I could not stand before You. But forgiveness is found with You, and I bow before You in wonder. Thank You for Your servant Gregory of Narek, who spoke to You with an honest heart and found that Your mercy is deeper than our sin. Give me courage to bring You what I have hidden. Teach me to wait for You as a guard waits for the morning. And bless Your people in every land who cry to You from the depths, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Gregory told God everything, the good and the bad. Is there anything you find hard to say to God? Why?
  • Why do you think Psalm 130 says that God’s forgiveness leads to awe, and not to carelessness?
  • Have the prayers of another believer ever given you words when you had none? What were they?

  • Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, especially “Book X”
  • Ochorus Originals, The Key Teachings of Richard Baxter, especially “Counsel for the Melancholy”

fields.title: Faith Seeking Your Face
fields.body_html:
“LORD, listen as I cry out to You; show me grace and answer me. My heart says to You what You have said: ‘Seek My face.’ So I will seek Your face, LORD.” (Psalm 27:7-8)

In the abbey of Bec, in Normandy in northern France, a monk could not stop thinking. It was around the year 1077. His name was Anselm, and he was the prior, the second leader of the monastery after the abbot. He had already written one book about God. Now he wanted to find a single, simple line of thought that would show that God truly exists and is the highest good.

He tells us himself what happened, in the preface to his little book. Sometimes the answer seemed “just within my reach.” Then it slipped away again. At last, he says, “in despair I was about to cease,” and he tried to put the whole question out of his mind, so that he could think about other things. But the thought would not leave him alone. It kept pressing on him, “with a kind of importunity,” that is, like a visitor who keeps knocking. Then one day, tired of fighting it, he saw the answer he had been looking for. He was full of joy, and he wrote it down.

What is surprising is how the book begins. Anselm was one of the best thinkers of his age. We might expect him to begin with an argument. Instead he begins with a prayer. He speaks first to himself, and then to God:

“Up now, slight man! flee, for a little while, thy occupations; hide thyself, for a time, from thy disturbing thoughts. Cast aside, now, thy burdensome cares, and put away thy toilsome business. Yield room for some little time to God; and rest for a little time in him. Enter the inner chamber of thy mind; shut out all thoughts save that of God, and such as can aid thee in seeking him; close thy door and seek him. Speak now, my whole heart! speak now to God, saying, I seek thy face; thy face, Lord, will I seek (Psalms xxvii. 8).”

Anselm, Proslogium, Monologium and Cur Deus Homo

The words at the end are from Psalm 27:8. Anselm, the great thinker, starts where David the psalmist started: with a heart that wants to see the face of God.

Who he was

Anselm was born in about 1033 in Aosta, a town in the Alps that is now part of northern Italy. As a young man he crossed the mountains and came to Bec, where a famous teacher named Lanfranc taught. At about twenty-seven he became a monk there. He was later made prior, and in 1078 the monks chose him as their abbot.

In 1093 he was made Archbishop of Canterbury, the leading bishop of England. His friend and secretary Eadmer, who wrote his life, says that he did not want the honor. It brought him many troubles. He would not let the kings of England control the church as they wished, and he was sent into exile twice. He died in 1109.

He wrote several books that are still studied today. One of the best known, Cur Deus Homo, asks why God became man. But the book in this chapter is the little one he wrote at Bec. He tells us that he first called it Faith Seeking Understanding. Later, at the request of others, he renamed it Proslogium, which means “a discourse,” or a speech addressed to someone. It is addressed to God.

How he prayed

Anselm wrote his book, he says, “in the person of one who strives to lift his mind to the contemplation of God, and seeks to understand what he believes.” So he did not write as someone outside the faith trying to decide if God is real. He wrote as a believer who loved God and wanted to know Him better.

His first chapter is a long, honest prayer. He tells God that he was made to see Him and has never yet seen Him. He feels like “an exile far from thee.” He knows that sin has spoiled the image of God in him. And then he asks God for help in the very search itself:

“Teach me to seek thee, and reveal thyself to me, when I seek thee, for I cannot seek thee, except thou teach me, nor find thee, except thou reveal thyself. Let me seek thee in longing, let me long for thee in seeking; let me find thee in love, and love thee in finding.”

Anselm, Proslogium, Monologium and Cur Deus Homo

He ends the chapter with the words he is most famous for: “I do not seek to understand that I may believe, but I believe in order to understand.” He learned this from Augustine, who had said something very like it long before. Faith comes first. Thinking and studying come after, and they help faith to grow.

Anselm also wrote a collection of prayers and meditations, and they were copied and loved for centuries. He seems to have prayed over ordinary sights as well. Francis de Sales, writing about five hundred years later, passed on a story about him. One day, as Anselm rode along, a hunted hare ran under his horse to hide from the dogs. His companions laughed, but “the great Anselm wept.” He said that the poor animal was like a soul in danger, with enemies all around and nowhere to run. Then he went on his way, sighing.

Your face I will seek

Look closely at Psalm 27:8. “My heart says to You what You have said: ‘Seek My face.’” The seeking begins with God. He speaks first: “Seek My face.” The heart hears Him and answers, “So I will seek Your face.”

In the Bible, to seek someone’s face means to come into their presence, to want them and not only their gifts. A child who has been away from home does not want only a gift from her father. She wants to see his face.

That is why Anselm’s prayer is so humble. He knew that he could not find God by his own cleverness. “I cannot seek thee, except thou teach me.” We pray because God has already spoken to us. Every prayer we offer is an answer to His invitation.

Anselm also shows us that loving God with the mind is part of prayer. Jesus told us to love God with all our heart, soul, mind and strength. Some believers fear that thinking hard about God will weaken their faith. Anselm thought hard, and his thinking made him pray more, not less.

Three key insights

  1. Even the best minds must ask God to teach them how to seek Him. Anselm was one of the great thinkers of his age, yet he prayed, “Teach me to seek thee.” We do not find God by cleverness. He shows Himself to those who ask.
  2. Faith and careful thinking are friends, and both can lead us to prayer. Anselm believed first and then studied in order to understand. His questions did not drive him away from God; they drove him to his knees.
  3. To meet God we must sometimes shut the door on our cares for a while. Anselm told his own soul to put away its busy thoughts and make room for God. A few quiet minutes, given wholly to God, can change the whole day.

For us today

Some readers of this book are students: in a university in Seoul, a Bible school in Kinshasa, a secondary school in Quito. You may be told that faith and study cannot go together. Anselm shows another way. You can bring your questions to God in prayer. He is not afraid of them.

Other readers are not students at all. You may be a farmer, a driver, or a mother who never finished school. Anselm’s prayer is for you too. “Teach me to seek You” is a prayer anyone can pray. You do not need a book or a library. You need only a heart that wants to see God’s face.

And all of us, rich or poor, need what Anselm called a little room for God. Our cares crowd in, our phones call to us, and our work never seems to end. Anselm tells us to close the door, even for a short time, and seek Him.

Try this

This week, let Anselm teach you to seek God’s face.

  • Close the door. Each day, set aside ten minutes. Before you pray, tell your soul, as Anselm did, to put down its cares for a while. Then shut the door, as Jesus taught in Matthew 6:6.
  • Pray Anselm’s prayer. Say slowly, “Lord, teach me to seek You, and show Yourself to me when I seek You.”
  • Bring one question. Write down one question about God or the Bible that troubles you. Bring it to God in prayer, and then look for the answer in Scripture or ask a wise believer.
  • Notice the hare. When you see something sad or beautiful in the street today, turn it into a short prayer, as Anselm did.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You have said to me, “Seek My face,” and my heart answers, “Your face, Lord, I will seek.” I cannot seek You unless You teach me, and I cannot find You unless You show Yourself to me. Thank You for Your servant Anselm, who believed in order to understand, and who loved You with his mind as well as his heart. Quiet my busy thoughts, and give me room to rest in You. Let me seek You in longing and long for You in seeking. Let me find You in love, and love You in finding, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Psalm 27:8 says that God speaks first: “Seek My face.” How does it change your prayer to know that God invited you?
  • Do you ever feel that thinking hard about God might weaken your faith? What does Anselm’s example teach you?
  • What “burdensome cares” do you need to put down for a while each day, so that you can make room for God?

fields.title: Jesus, the Very Thought of You
fields.body_html:
“We love because He loved us first.” (1 John 4:19)

In the spring of the year 1113, a group of about thirty young men came to the gate of a monastery in Burgundy, in eastern France. The monastery was called Cîteaux. It was new, poor and very strict. Its monks wanted to keep the old Rule of Benedict exactly, with long hours of prayer, hard work in the fields, plain food and silence. Few people wanted to join them. Some feared that the little community would die out.

Then these young men arrived, most of them from noble families, and asked to be let in. Their leader was about twenty-two years old. His name was Bernard. Many of the others were his own relatives: his brothers, an uncle and friends he had persuaded to come with him. One of his friends, William of Saint-Thierry, later wrote the first part of his life. He tells how Bernard went from house to house, speaking about Christ so warmly that mothers hid their sons from him and wives their husbands, for fear that they too would follow him into the monastery.

The story is told that as the brothers left their family home, the eldest said to the youngest, a boy still playing in the street, that all the family land would now be his. The boy answered that this was not a fair division: they were taking heaven and leaving him only the earth. Some years later he followed them too.

Two years after Bernard arrived, the abbot of Cîteaux sent him with twelve monks to start a new house in a wild valley. Bernard named it Clairvaux, which means “clear valley” or “valley of light.” He was its abbot for the rest of his life. The first years were very hard, and the monks often had little to eat. But they kept the hours of prayer, by day and by night, and more and more men came to join them.

Who he was

Bernard of Clairvaux became one of the best-known Christians of his age. He wrote hundreds of letters and gave advice to kings and popes. One of his own monks became Pope Eugene III. He preached so sweetly about Christ that later generations called him the “honey-sweet teacher.” Many Protestants have loved him too. John Calvin quoted him again and again.

But at the center of his life was not politics. It was love for Jesus. He gave more than eighty sermons on a single short book of the Bible, the Song of Songs, which he read as a picture of the love between Christ and the soul. He died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153, after forty years as a monk.

Why we love God

Some time around 1128 (the exact date is uncertain), Haimeric, a cardinal and the chancellor of the church of Rome, asked Bernard two questions: Why should we love God? And how much? Bernard answered with a short book called On Loving God. His first answer is famous:

“I should say that God Himself is the motive of our love to Him, and that the measure of due love is to be without measure.”

Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God

In other words, we love God because of who He is, and there is no point at which we have loved Him enough. And why does God have a right to our love? Bernard’s answer is the verse at the top of this chapter: “Especially this, that He first loved us.” John says the same: “This is where love is found: not in our having loved God, but in His loving us and sending His Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

Bernard then describes four steps, or “degrees,” of love. At first we love only ourselves. Then, when trouble comes, we learn to love God for what He gives us. This is where prayer often begins. We cry to God because we need Him. But Bernard says something wonderful happens as we keep coming:

“Let the frequency of trials bring us often to the feet of God, surely it is impossible, but we must begin to know Him, and, knowing Him, must come to discern His sweetness.”

Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God

The old English is a little hard. Bernard means that when our troubles bring us to God again and again, we cannot help getting to know Him, and once we know Him, we taste how good He is. So we reach the third step: we love God not only for His gifts but for Himself. The fourth step, loving even ourselves only for God’s sake, Bernard thought we reach only rarely in this life, and fully only in heaven.

The very thought of Jesus

Many English-speaking Christians know Bernard’s name from a hymn. In 1849 Edward Caswall translated an old Latin poem, Jesu dulcis memoria, which means “the sweet memory of Jesus.” In the 1873 edition of his Hymns and Poems it begins: “Jesu! the very thought of Thee / With sweetness fills my breast; / But sweeter far thy face to see, / And in thy presence rest.”

For centuries the poem was credited to Bernard. Most scholars now think it was probably written by an unknown writer of his time, or a little after, who loved his teaching. But it sounds very much like him. Here is how Bernard himself spoke of the name of Jesus in one of his sermons, as John Calvin quoted him four hundred years later:

“The name of Jesus is not only light but food also, yea, oil, without which all the food of the soul is dry; salt, without which as a condiment whatever is set before us is insipid; in fine, honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, joy in the heart, and, at the same time, medicine; every discourse where this name is not heard is absurd”

John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion

A shadow on his life

We must be honest. Bernard was a great lover of Christ, but he was not perfect. In 1146, at the pope’s request, he preached the Second Crusade, a war to defend the Christian kingdoms in the Holy Land. At Vézelay in France he spoke to a huge crowd, and thousands promised to go. The crusade ended in terrible failure, and many thousands died. Bernard was deeply grieved, and many blamed him.

To his credit, when a monk named Radulf stirred up crowds in Germany to attack and kill Jews, Bernard traveled there, stopped him and sent him back to his monastery. Even so, many Christians today look back on the crusades with sorrow. Bernard reminds us that even those who pray most can be carried along by the passions of their time, and they too need God’s mercy.

Three key insights

  1. Our love for God is always an answer to His love for us. “We love because He loved us first.” We never begin the relationship; we only respond to a love that was there before us.
  2. Troubles that drive us to God can teach us to love Him for Himself. Bernard saw that we often begin to pray because we need help. But as we keep coming, we taste God’s goodness, and we start to love the Giver more than His gifts.
  3. Even the holiest believers need God’s mercy for their mistakes. Bernard’s love for Christ was real, and so was his error in preaching war. His life teaches us to pray humbly and to ask God to show us the faults we cannot see in ourselves.

For us today

Bernard’s steps of love are a map for ordinary believers. A young man in Lagos first prays because he needs a job. A widow in Lima first prays because she is lonely. That is not a bad beginning. God welcomes needy people. But He wants to lead us further, until we love Him simply because He is good.

Bernard also invites us to think about Jesus during the day. A hymn, a short verse or simply His name can turn a long bus ride or a day in the market into a time of worship.

And Bernard’s shadow speaks to us too. In many lands today, Christians feel the pull of anger toward people of another faith or tribe. The love of Christ calls us to bless and pray for them.

Try this

This week, let Bernard teach you to love God for Himself.

  • Start with His love. Each morning, before you ask God for anything, read 1 John 4:19 and thank Him for one way He has loved you first.
  • Climb a step. In your prayers, notice how much is asking for gifts. Then spend a few minutes praising God simply for who He is.
  • Carry His name. Choose one line, such as “Jesus, the very thought of You fills my heart with joy,” and pray it quietly through the day.
  • Pray for peace. Pray for one people or group your nation has been in conflict with, and ask God to bless them.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, I love You because You loved me first. Before I ever called on You, You came for me, lived for me, died for me and rose again. Thank You for Your servant Bernard, who loved Your name and taught Your church that the measure of loving You is to love without measure. When troubles bring me to Your feet, let me taste how good You are, and learn to love You for Yourself. Forgive me where, like him, I have been carried along by the angers of my time. Let the very thought of You fill my heart with joy, until I see Your face. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Bernard says the measure of loving God is to love Him “without measure.” What would that look like in your life this week?
  • Think of a time when trouble brought you to prayer. Did you come to know God better through it?
  • What can we learn from the fact that a man who loved Jesus so deeply also made a serious mistake?
