fields.title: Praise for Brother Sun
fields.body_html:
“Sun and moon, praise Him! All shining stars, praise Him!” (Psalm 148:3)

In the year 1225, a sick man lay in a small hut beside the church of San Damiano, just outside the town of Assisi in central Italy. He was about forty-three years old, but his body was worn out. His stomach was weak. His eyes were so diseased that he could hardly bear the light of the sun or of a fire, and he was nearly blind. At night, the old stories say, mice ran over him so that he could not sleep.

His name was Francis. Nearly twenty years before, as a young man, he had prayed in this same little church and given his life to Christ. Now the women who followed his way of life, led by his friend Clare, lived at San Damiano, and they cared for him as best they could.

Thomas of Celano, a friar who knew him and wrote two accounts of his life within about twenty years of his death, tells what happened (the Mirror of Perfection, a later collection of stories from his first companions, places it here at San Damiano). One night, in great pain, Francis prayed for help to bear his sufferings patiently. He seemed to hear the Lord promise him the kingdom of heaven, and he was filled with joy. Then, Celano says, “he composed certain ‘Praises concerning the Creatures,’ inciting them in some sort to praise the Creator.”

The song he made is known today as the Canticle of Brother Sun, or the Canticle of the Creatures. Francis wrote it not in Latin, the language of the church, but in the everyday speech of his own region, so that ordinary people could sing it. It is one of the oldest poems we have in the Italian language. Here is how it begins in an old English translation:

“O most high, almighty, good Lord God, to thee belong praise, glory, honor, and all blessing! ... Praised be my Lord God with all his creatures, and specially our brother the sun, who brings us the day and who brings us the light; fair is he and shines with a very great splendor: O Lord, he signifies to us thee!”

The song goes on to praise God for “our sister the moon, and for the stars,” for brother wind, sister water, brother fire and “our mother the earth.” A man who could hardly see the sun sang God’s praise for it.

Who he was

Francis was born in Assisi in about 1181 or 1182. His father, Pietro Bernardone, was a rich cloth merchant. As a young man Francis loved parties, fine clothes and dreams of being a knight. He went to war with the nearby town of Perugia, was taken prisoner and spent about a year in prison. After he came home he grew ill and restless.

One day he was praying before a painted cross in the ruined church of San Damiano. G. K. Chesterton tells the story: he heard a voice saying to him, “Francis, seest thou not that my house is in ruins? Go and restore it for me.” Francis began by mending the walls with his own hands. Later he understood that God was calling him to help renew His church. He gave up his inheritance, chose to live in poverty like Christ, and began to preach. Soon others joined him. They became the Friars Minor, the “lesser brothers,” known today as Franciscans.

He traveled and preached across Italy. In 1219 he even crossed into a war zone in Egypt to speak about Christ to the Sultan. He died on 3 October 1226, singing, his brothers say, and greeting death as a sister. Celano records that he said, “Welcome, my sister Death.”

How he prayed

Celano says that Francis “made a temple of his breast.” In a crowd, if he felt God near, he would cover his face with his cloak or his sleeve to pray unseen. In the woods he wept, sighed and spoke with God aloud. Celano’s summary is one of the most famous lines ever written about a person at prayer: the whole man was “not so much praying, as having become a [living] prayer.”

Francis also prayed with his eyes open. Celano says that he was filled with joy “as he beheld the sun, or raised his eyes to the moon, or gazed on the stars, and the firmament.” He called every creature his brother or sister, because the same Father had made them all. And he did not forget this even in pain. Chesterton tells how, near the end, doctors decided to treat his eyes with a red-hot iron:

“When they took the brand from the furnace, he rose as with an urbane gesture and spoke as to an invisible presence: “Brother Fire, God made you beautiful and strong and useful; I pray you be courteous with me.””

G. K. Chesterton, St. Francis of Assisi

“Courteous” means gentle and kind. Francis spoke even to the fire as a fellow creature of God.

All creation praising

Psalm 148 calls on everything God has made to praise Him: angels, “sun and moon,” “all shining stars,” sea creatures, snow, wind, mountains, trees, animals, kings and “young men and young women alike, the old together with the young!” (Psalm 148:12). Celano compared Francis to the three young men in the fiery furnace who, in an old song that is added to the book of Daniel in the Greek Bible, called on all creation to bless the Lord. That song echoes this very psalm.

Francis did not worship the sun. He praised the God who made it. The sun, he sang, “signifies to us” the Most High. Creation is like a window through which we see the Creator’s goodness.

Near the end of his life, Francis added two more verses. When the bishop and the mayor of Assisi were quarreling bitterly, he wrote a verse praising God for “all those who pardon one another for his love’s sake,” and sent his brothers to sing it before them both. The Mirror of Perfection says the two men were moved and made peace. And when Francis knew he was dying, he added a last verse praising God for “our sister, the death of the body.”

A prayer that is not his

Many people know a beautiful prayer that begins, “Lord, make me an instrument of Your peace.” It is often called the Prayer of Saint Francis. But it is not found in any of his writings. The earliest known copy was printed in a small French Catholic magazine in 1912, and it was linked with Francis only a few years later, when it was printed on the back of a card bearing his picture. It is a fine prayer, and it fits his spirit well. But if we want his own words, the Canticle of Brother Sun is the place to begin.

Three key insights

  1. All creation is a choir of praise, and prayer lets us join in. Psalm 148 calls on sun, moon and stars to praise God. Francis taught us to see every creature as a reason to thank our Maker.
  2. We can thank God for His gifts even when we can no longer enjoy them. Francis sang his song of the sun when he could hardly see it. Thanksgiving does not wait until life is easy.
  3. Praise can become a peacemaker. Francis used a song to bring two enemies together. When we praise God together, it is harder to keep hating one another.

For us today

Francis was rich and became poor by choice. Many readers of this book are poor without choosing it. Francis reminds us that the sun rises on rich and poor alike. A farmer in Uganda, a fisherman in Indonesia, a street seller in Bogotá can all lift their eyes each morning and praise the Maker of the sun.

Francis also challenges us to care for the earth God made. If the water is our sister, we should not poison her. If the earth is our mother, we should not waste her gifts.

And his song speaks to those who are sick. Some of you read this from a hospital bed or a dark room. Francis wrote his greatest praise when he was weakest.

Try this

This week, let Francis teach you to praise God with all creation.

  • Greet the sun. When you see the sunrise or sunset, stop and say, “Praise be to You, my Lord, for Brother Sun.”
  • Pray Psalm 148. Read it aloud slowly. Look out of a window and name the things you see that praise God.
  • Write your own verse. Add a line to Francis’s song for something in your own land: “Praised be my Lord for Sister Rain,” or “for Brother Mango Tree.”
  • Make peace with a song. If there is a quarrel in your home or church, gather people to sing a hymn of praise together, and then talk.

A closing prayer

Most high, almighty and good Lord, all praise, glory and honor belong to You. Thank You for the sun and moon and all the shining stars, for wind and water, fire and earth, which You made and which praise You. Thank You for Your servant Francis, who became poor for Christ’s sake and sang Your praise even in pain. Open my eyes to see Your goodness in all You have made. Teach me to give thanks in the dark as well as in the light. Make me a peacemaker, and when my last day comes, let me meet it in peace, trusting in Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Francis sang about the sun when he could hardly see it. What would it mean for you to praise God in your present troubles?
  • How does seeing the sun, the rain or the stars help you to pray?
  • Why do you think praising God together can help people to forgive one another?

  • Ochorus Originals, The Key Teachings of G. K. Chesterton, especially “The Holy Joy of St Francis”

fields.title: Gazing on Christ
fields.body_html:
“But all of us, our faces uncovered, look upon the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and we are being changed into the same image we see, from glory to ever greater glory. That is how the Lord, who is the Spirit, works.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Sometime around the year 1234, a letter left a small convent outside Assisi in Italy. Messengers carried it north, over the Alps, on roads that were long and often dangerous. They were going to Prague, the royal city of Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic.

The letter was addressed to a princess. Her name was Agnes. She was the daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia, and she had been offered marriage to some of the greatest men in Europe, the Emperor Frederick II among them. She had refused them all. Instead she had built a hospital for the poor in Prague and a convent beside it, and she was about to enter it herself, to live in poverty and prayer.

The writer of the letter had never met her. She was a woman of about forty, living in a poor house beside the little church of San Damiano. Her name was Clare, and she had cared for Francis there when he was sick and nearly blind. She had heard of Agnes, and she wrote to encourage her. Over the next twenty years she wrote to Agnes again and again. Four of her letters to Agnes have survived, and scholars accept them as truly hers. The two women never saw each other’s faces in this life. But they prayed for each other, and they shared one desire: to look at Jesus Christ and to become like Him.

In one letter Clare writes, in a translation made in 1910, “Look, O most noble Queen, upon your Spouse.” By “Spouse” she means Christ, who loves His people as a husband loves his bride. Look at Him, she says. See how He who was more beautiful than any man was beaten and shamed and died on the cross for you. In another letter she urges Agnes to “place your mind in the mirror of eternity,” and “in contemplating God transform yourself into an image of His Deity.”

In what seems to be her last letter, written perhaps near the end of her life, she comes back to the same picture: “Every day look into this mirror, O Queen, spouse of Christ Jesus, and often contemplate your countenance therein.” The mirror is Christ. When we look at Him, we also see ourselves truly, and we are changed.

Who she was

Clare was born in Assisi in 1194 into a noble family. As a girl she heard Francis preach, and she longed to give her life to Christ in the same way. On the night of Palm Sunday in 1212, at seventeen, she slipped out of her father’s house and went to the little chapel where Francis and his brothers lived. There she gave her life to God, and they cut off her long hair as a sign. Her family came to drag her home, but she would not go. Soon her younger sister Agnes joined her, and in later years her mother as well.

Clare and her sisters settled at San Damiano, and she lived there for the rest of her life, about forty-one years. They owned nothing. They worked with their hands, cared for one another and prayed through the day and night. For many years Clare herself was ill, often unable to rise from her bed. Yet she wrote a Rule for her sisters, the first rule for a religious community known to have been written by a woman. The pope approved it on 9 August 1253. Two days later, on 11 August, she died.

How she prayed

Soon after her death, someone wrote a Legend of Saint Clare, which means “the story of her life to be read aloud.” It was long credited to Thomas of Celano, though no one is sure who wrote it. It says that after the evening prayers, when her tired sisters went to their hard beds, she “watched thus ever at night and was never weary of praying to God.” When she came from prayer, the sisters said, “her countenance was more beautiful and more bright after her prayer than before.” Like Moses coming down from the mountain, her face seemed to show that she had been with God.

The Legend also tells a famous story. In 1240, soldiers in the army of the Emperor, among them Muslim soldiers whom the writers call Saracens, attacked San Damiano and broke into the convent grounds. The sisters ran to Clare in terror. She was sick, so she had herself carried to the door, with the bread of the Lord’s Supper, kept in a small container, carried before her. There she lay on the ground and prayed with tears for her sisters. The Legend says she heard a voice like a child’s answer, “I will keep you always,” and the soldiers fled.

We should hold the details of this story gently. It comes from a book written to honor a saint, and later artists added more, painting Clare herself holding up a monstrance, a special vessel for showing the bread, before the soldiers. The heart of the story is simpler: a sick woman, unable to fight, turned to Christ in prayer when danger came.

Her last words, as the Legend gives them, were words of thanks: “Good Lord God, blessed art Thou who created me.”

Changed by looking

Paul wrote 2 Corinthians 3:18 with Moses in mind. When Moses spoke with God, his face shone, and he covered it with a veil. But in Christ, Paul says, all of us look upon the Lord’s glory “our faces uncovered.” Not only great leaders. All of us. And as we look, “we are being changed into the same image we see.”

That is Clare’s teaching. We become like what we look at. If we fill our eyes with anger, we grow angry. If we fill them with Christ, we slowly become like Him. The change is not quick. Paul says it goes “from glory to ever greater glory.” And it is not our own work: “That is how the Lord, who is the Spirit, works.”

Andrew Murray, the South African pastor, taught the same thing about faith in prayer:

“So believing God is just looking to God and what He is, allowing Him to reveal His presence, giving Him time and yielding the whole being to take in the full impression of what He is as God, the soul opened up to receive and rejoice in the overshadowing of His love.”

Andrew Murray, With Christ in the School of Prayer

Clare was enclosed in one small house for forty years. Some would say her life was small. But she spent it looking at Christ, and her prayers and letters have helped believers ever since.

Three key insights

  1. We become like the One we look at. Paul says that as we look upon the Lord’s glory, we are changed into His image. Prayer that simply gazes on Christ with love is one of the ways God makes us like His Son.
  2. Friends who pray for one another can strengthen each other across great distances. Clare and Agnes never met, yet their letters and prayers held each other up for twenty years. Distance cannot stop the prayers of God’s people.
  3. A hidden life of prayer is never a wasted life. Clare spent forty years in one small convent, often sick in bed. God used her quiet faithfulness to bless many people she never saw.

For us today

Many readers cannot leave their homes. Some are old or sick. Some care for a family member all day long. Some live where it is not safe to go out to church. Clare shows that a small room can be a place of great prayer. A grandmother in a village in Ethiopia, praying on her mat, may be doing more for the church than she knows.

Clare’s letters also speak to believers far from one another. A worker in the Gulf writes to her sister in Kerala. A student in China sends messages to a friend in Kenya. Our messages can do what Clare’s letters did: point one another to Christ.

And in a world full of screens and pictures, Clare asks us a simple question: what are we looking at most? Our eyes shape our hearts.

Try this

This week, let Clare teach you to look at Christ.

  • Look into the mirror. Each day, read one short story about Jesus from the Gospels. Then sit quietly for five minutes and simply look at Him in your mind, without asking for anything.
  • Watch your eyes. Notice what you look at most during the day. Choose one thing to look at less, and give that time to Christ.
  • Write a Clare letter. Write or send a message to a believer far away. Tell them you are praying for them, and point them to Jesus.
  • Pray for those who cannot go out. Pray for the sick, the old and the persecuted who pray in small rooms.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus Christ, You are the mirror of God’s glory. Thank You for Your servant Clare, who looked at You with love all her life, in poverty, in sickness and in danger. Uncover my face, and let me look upon Your glory. Change me into Your image, from glory to ever greater glory, by Your Holy Spirit. Strengthen my friends who are far away, and let our prayers hold one another up. When my life seems small and hidden, remind me that nothing done for You is wasted. And at the end, let me also say, “Blessed are You, my God, who created me.” Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Paul says we are changed as we look at the Lord’s glory. What helps you to “look” at Christ in prayer?
  • Clare and Agnes never met, yet they helped each other for twenty years. Who could you encourage in faith from far away?
  • Clare lived most of her life in one small place. Do you ever feel your life is too small to matter to God? What would Clare say to you?

  • Ochorus Originals, The Key Teachings of A. W. Tozer, especially “The Gaze of the Soul”

fields.title: A Prayer Before Study
fields.body_html:
“If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to you.” (James 1:5)

In the autumn of 1273, in the Dominican house at Naples in southern Italy, a large, quiet friar was working on the greatest book of his life. His name was Thomas, and he came from the family of the counts of Aquino, so the world knows him as Thomas Aquinas. For eight years he had been writing a huge work called the Summa Theologiae, a “summary of theology,” meant to set out the whole Christian faith in order for students.

The early accounts say that before he studied, taught, wrote or dictated, he first went aside to pray. When he came to a hard passage of Scripture, he added fasting to his prayer. His closest friend and secretary was a friar named Reginald of Piperno. Thomas once told Reginald, as the old Catholic Encyclopedia sums up the early witnesses, “that he had learned more in prayer and contemplation than he had acquired from men or books.”

Then, on 6 December 1273, something happened. Thomas was saying Mass in the chapel of Saint Nicholas, and he was there a very long time, lost in God. Afterward he put away his pen and his writing materials. He would not write, and he would not dictate.

Reginald was alarmed. The Summa was not finished. He begged Thomas to go on. We have Thomas’s answer from a witness named Bartholomew of Capua, who heard it from Reginald and told it under oath in 1319, when the church was gathering evidence before declaring Thomas a saint. Thomas said that he could not, because everything he had written now seemed to him like straw, compared with what had been shown to him.

Straw holds up the grain while it grows, but it is not the grain. Thomas, the most learned man of his age, had glimpsed something of God so great that all his careful pages looked small beside it.

Early in 1274 he set out for a church council at Lyon in France, but fell ill on the way. He died at the abbey of Fossanova on 7 March 1274. His great book was never finished.

Who he was

Thomas was born around 1225 in the castle of Roccasecca, between Rome and Naples. When he was about five, his parents sent him to the great monastery of Monte Cassino, which Benedict had founded seven hundred years before (we met Benedict in chapter 1). His teachers remembered a quiet child who often asked one question: “What is God?” He spent the rest of his life trying to answer it.

As a young man he chose to join the Dominicans, a new order of poor preaching friars. His noble family was furious. His brothers seized him on the road and kept him shut up at home for about a year. He would not change his mind, and at last he was let go. He studied in Paris and in Cologne under Albert the Great. The story is told that the other students called him “the dumb ox,” because he was big and silent, and that Albert said one day the world would hear this ox bellow.

He became the most famous teacher in Europe. He wrote commentaries on many books of the Bible, and hymns traditionally credited to him are still sung. Popes wanted him near them. Yet he refused to become archbishop of Naples, and he stayed a simple friar to the end.

The Catholic Church honors him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. Protestants and Orthodox have disagreed with parts of his thought, and some Reformers argued with him sharply, but many have admired his clear mind and his humility. What we learn from him here belongs to all of us: he would not study about God without first speaking to God.

How he prayed

A prayer for students has long been prayed in his name. It begins in Latin with the words Creator ineffabilis, “Creator beyond words.” It is traditionally attributed to Thomas, but we cannot prove that he wrote it himself. But it fits what his friends said about him. In our own plain English, it runs something like this:

Creator beyond all words, from the treasures of Your wisdom You set the angels in their wonderful order and arranged every part of the universe with great beauty. You are the true fountain of light and wisdom, the first beginning of all things. Pour a ray of Your brightness into the darkness of my mind. Take from me the double darkness into which I was born: sin and ignorance. You make the tongues of little children speak well: train my tongue, and pour the grace of Your blessing on my lips. Give me a sharp mind to understand, a strong memory to keep what I learn, a good way of learning and ease in it, skill to explain, and grace in speaking. Guide the beginning of my work, direct its progress, and bring it to completion. You are true God and true man, and You live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.

Notice what the prayer asks for. It does not ask to be clever or famous. It asks God to drive away two kinds of darkness: ignorance, which study can help, and sin, which only God can forgive. A proud heart can darken a brilliant mind.

Catherine of Siena, whom we will meet in chapter 14, was born about seventy years after Thomas died. In her book The Dialogue, she writes down what she believed God had shown her in prayer, and she names Thomas there:

“With this light that is given to the eye of the intellect, Thomas Aquinas saw Me, wherefore he acquired the light of much science; also Augustine, Jerome, and the doctors, and my saints.”

Catherine of Siena, The Dialogue

By “science” she means knowledge. The great teachers understood the Scriptures because God gave them light.

Wisdom from above

James wrote to ordinary believers, many of them poor and suffering. He told them that if they lacked wisdom, they should “ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding” (James 1:5). God does not sigh when we come to Him again. He does not say, “You should know this by now.” He gives gladly.

James adds: “But you must ask in faith, without wavering” (James 1:6). Thomas asked God for understanding, and then he worked hard. Both were needed. Proverbs says, “For it is the LORD who gives wisdom; knowledge and understanding come from His mouth” (Proverbs 2:6).

Charles Spurgeon gave the same counsel to everyone who studies the Bible:

“Stones are not broken except by an earnest use of the hammer. And the stone-breaker usually goes down on his knees. Use the hammer of diligence and let the knees of prayer be exercised, too, and there is not a stony doctrine in Revelation which is useful for you to understand which will not fly into shivers under the exercise of prayer and faith.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Mighty Power in Prayer

By “Revelation” Spurgeon means all that God has revealed in the Bible.

Three key insights

  1. Before we study about God, we should speak to God. Thomas went aside to pray before he taught or wrote. Knowledge of God grows best in a heart that is talking with Him.
  2. God gives wisdom gladly to everyone who asks Him in faith. James promises that God gives with an open hand and without scolding. No question is too small, and no learner is too slow.
  3. All our learning is straw beside the glory of God Himself. At the end, Thomas saw that God is far greater than his books. Study is good, but it should humble us and lead us to worship.

For us today

You do not need to be a scholar to pray Thomas’s prayer. A schoolgirl in Nairobi facing an exam, a farmer in Bolivia learning to read, a pastor in a village in Myanmar preparing a sermon with one worn Bible, a nurse in Chennai studying at night after a long shift: each of them needs wisdom, and each of them can ask.

James’s promise also covers problems that books cannot solve: a family conflict, a hard choice about work, a decision about where to live.

And Thomas’s last months speak to those who have many books, studies and online teachings. Knowledge is a gift, but Paul warns that “knowledge puffs a person up, but love builds others up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The test of our learning is whether it makes us love God and our neighbor more.

Try this

This week, let prayer come before your work of learning.

  • Pray before you open a book. Before you study for school, prepare a lesson or learn something for your job, stop and ask God for light, even in one sentence.
  • Pray Thomas’s prayer. Use the plain English version above, or make your own: “Lord, take away my darkness. Help me to understand, to remember and to explain.”
  • Bring one hard question to God. Write down a question about your faith or your life, and ask God for wisdom about it each day.
  • Let learning lead to worship. When you understand something new about God, stop and thank Him for it.

A closing prayer

Father of lights, You give wisdom to everyone who asks, with an open hand and without scolding. I am short of wisdom, and I come to You. Take from me the darkness of sin and the darkness of ignorance. Give me a mind to understand Your word, a memory to keep it, and words to share it with others. Bless the work of my hands and of my mind, from its beginning to its end. Keep me humble, and when I have learned all I can, let me see that You are greater still. Thank You for Your servant Thomas, who prayed before he studied. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Thomas prayed before he studied, taught or wrote. What work in your life could you begin with prayer?
  • James says God gives wisdom “without scolding.” Why do you think we sometimes feel afraid to ask God for help?
  • What do you think Thomas meant when he said his writing seemed like straw? How can learning make us either proud or humble?

  • E. M. Bounds, Power Through Prayer, especially “Heart Preparation Necessary”
  • Andrew Murray, The Inner Chamber, especially “The Heart and the Understanding”

fields.title: A Simple Reaching for God
fields.body_html:
“Who else is there for me in heaven? And having You, I want nothing on earth.” (Psalm 73:25)

Somewhere in England, in the later 1300s, a Christian teacher sat down to write a book for a young friend. We do not know the writer’s name. We do not know the young man’s name either. The book suggests that he was about twenty-four years old, and that God had drawn him step by step away from his worldly friends into a life given to prayer.

The young man wanted to know how to pray. The book assumes that he had already read and thought about God, and meditated on his sins and on the sufferings of Christ. Now he was hungry for something simpler and deeper: not to think about God only, but to reach God Himself in love.

So his teacher wrote to him, beginning with the words “Ghostly friend in God.” (“Ghostly” was the old English word for “spiritual.”) And he told him plainly what would happen when he tried to pray this way. At first, he warned, you will find only darkness, “and as it were a cloud of unknowing, thou knowest not what, saving that thou feelest in thy will a naked intent unto God.”

A “naked intent” is a bare purpose: a will that reaches out for God and nothing else, with nothing wrapped around it. The teacher did not tell his friend to wait until the darkness lifted. He told him to stay in it, and to keep crying out after the One he loved. God is so great, he explained, that no human mind can take Him in. Between us and God there is always, in this life, a kind of cloud. We cannot think our way through it. But love can reach where thought cannot. In the words of the book, “By love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never.”

And so the teacher gave his friend a picture he would never forget. When you pray, he said, “smite upon that thick cloud of unknowing with a sharp dart of longing love,” and do not give up, whatever happens.

The book that the nameless teacher wrote is called The Cloud of Unknowing. It became one of the best-known books on prayer ever written in English.

The book and its world

The Cloud of Unknowing was written in the English of its day, in the Midlands of England, probably in the second half of the 1300s. Scholars have long tried to discover its author. Many think he was a priest, and some think he was a Carthusian monk, a member of an order that lived in silence. But no one knows for certain. He seems to have wanted it that way: the book points away from its writer toward God.

It was a hard time to be alive in England. The Black Death had swept through the land in 1348 and 1349 and came back again and again, killing perhaps a third of the people or more. War with France dragged on for decades. In 1381 the peasants rose up in revolt. In the same years, in the city of Norwich, a woman named Julian was praying in a small room beside a church. We will meet her in chapter 13.

Into that frightened world the Cloud spoke of a love for God so simple that a busy, suffering person could practice it. In 1912 the English writer Evelyn Underhill published an edition in easier spelling, and many readers came to know it through her.

How it teaches us to pray

The heart of the book is easy to say. When you pray, lift your heart to God with love, and want God Himself, not only what He gives. The American pastor A. W. Tozer loved this old book. In The Pursuit of God he quoted its third chapter:

“Lift up thine heart unto God with a meek stirring of love; and mean Himself, and none of His goods.”

The Cloud of Unknowing, quoted in A. W. Tozer, The Pursuit of God

To “mean Himself” is to aim at God Himself. Many of our prayers are lists of things we want from God. The Cloud does not forbid that; Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread. But it says there is a deeper prayer, in which we want God more than any gift.

How can the mind hold on in such prayer, when it keeps wandering off? The Cloud gives very practical advice, which Tozer also loved. If you wish, it says, wrap up your whole longing for God in one word: “take thee but a little word of one syllable,” for the shorter it is, the better. “And such a word is this word GOD or this word LOVE.” Choose the one you like best, the writer adds, and fasten it to your heart. When distracting thoughts come, the book says, beat them down with this word. Do not argue with them. Simply turn back to God with your short word of love.

The writer explains why short prayers can be so strong. If a man is suddenly afraid of a fire, he does not make a long speech. He cries out one word: “fire!” That one word wakes everyone who hears it. In the same way, he says, “short prayer pierceth heaven,” when it comes from the depth of the heart.

Balance and a caution

Some have taken books like this as if they taught people to empty their minds, or to set aside the Bible and seek feelings instead. Tozer himself said that some of the old mystics needed careful reading. But the Cloud is more careful than its critics sometimes think. It writes for people who already know and love Christ. It explains that the God we reach for is “God that made thee, and bought thee,” that is, the Creator who redeemed us through Christ. And it says that beginners must be busy with “Reading, Thinking, and Praying”: hearing God’s word, thinking about it, and then praying. The simple reaching of love grows out of that soil, not instead of it.

Psalm 73 shows the same road. Its writer, Asaph, almost lost his faith when he saw wicked people doing well. Trying to understand it only wore him out: “it seemed a weary task to me” (Psalm 73:16). Then he went into God’s sanctuary and met God Himself. At the end he could say, “Who else is there for me in heaven? And having You, I want nothing on earth” (Psalm 73:25). He did not understand everything. But he had God, and that was enough.

Tozer saw the danger of wanting God plus something else:

“If we omit the ‘and’ we shall soon find God, and in Him we shall find that for which we have all our lives been secretly longing.”

A. W. Tozer, The Pursuit of God

Three key insights

  1. Love can reach God where our thinking cannot. We will never fully understand God in this life. But we can love Him and reach out to Him, even in the dark.
  2. Having God Himself is enough, even when we cannot understand His ways. Asaph could not make sense of the world around him. But in God’s presence he found that having God was better than anything on earth.
  3. One short word of love from the heart can pierce heaven. We do not need many words to pray. A single word like “God” or “love,” meant with all our heart, is heard.

For us today

Many believers think that real prayer must be long, clever or full of beautiful words. The Cloud sets them free. A tired mother in a crowded flat in Cairo, a miner in Zambia, a student in a dormitory in Seoul, an old man in a village in Guatemala who cannot read: any of them can turn to God with one word of love.

The book also helps those who feel that God is far away. Many Christians go through times when prayer feels dark and empty, and they think they have failed. The Cloud says that darkness is normal. The cloud is not a sign that God has left. It is a sign that God is greater than our minds. Keep reaching for Him.

And it speaks to all of us who have more than we need. Asaph envied the rich. We are often tempted to want God and something else: God and comfort, God and success. The Cloud invites us to want Him first.

Try this

This week, practice a simple reaching for God.

  • Choose your word. Pick one short word for God, such as “God,” “love” or “Jesus,” in your own language.
  • Sit and reach. For five minutes each day, sit quietly. Lift your heart to God with love, and hold your word gently. When your thoughts wander, do not fight them. Simply say your word and turn back.
  • Read first. Before you sit, read a few verses of Scripture, such as Psalm 73:23-26. Let God’s word fill your mind before you reach for Him in love.
  • Pray in a moment of need. When you are afraid or rushed this week, pray just one word from your heart, as a person cries “fire!”

A closing prayer

Lord God, You are greater than my mind can understand, and yet You let me love You. When I cannot see You, let me reach for You. When my thoughts wander, draw my heart back to You. I do not want only Your gifts; I want You. Who else is there for me in heaven? And having You, I want nothing on earth. You made me, You bought me with the blood of Your Son, and You have called me to Yourself. Take my small word of love and let it reach You. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Have you ever felt that God was hidden, as if behind a cloud? What helped you keep praying?
  • What is the difference between wanting God’s gifts and wanting God Himself?
  • Which short word would you choose for your prayer, and why?

fields.title: Waiting in Stillness
fields.body_html:
“The LORD is good to all who wait in hope for Him, to anyone who seeks Him. It is good to wait in silence for the LORD’s salvation.” (Lamentations 3:25-26)

Around the year 1316, a young man of about twenty left the city of Constantinople and sailed west to a mountain by the sea. His name was Gregory Palamas. His father had served at the court of the Byzantine emperor, and after his father died the emperor himself helped to raise the clever boy. Everyone expected him to become a great man in the government.

Instead he went to Mount Athos, a long, rocky peninsula in northern Greece that runs out into the Aegean Sea, with a high peak at its end. For more than three hundred years it had been a place of monks. Great monasteries stood along its shores, and smaller groups and hermits lived in huts and caves on its slopes. Gregory became a novice at the monastery of Vatopedi. Later he moved to the Great Lavra, the oldest of the great monasteries, where he served in the dining hall and sang in the church. Later still he went to live in a small, quiet settlement of monks, to give himself more fully to prayer.

On Athos he learned a way of praying that the monks called hesychia. It is a Greek word meaning stillness, or quiet. Those who practiced it were called hesychasts, “people of stillness.”

A hesychast did not seek quiet in order to empty his mind. He sought it in order to be with Christ. Often he would sit on a low stool in his cell, in the dark hours of the night or early morning. He bowed his head. He let his breathing grow slow and calm. And he gathered his scattered thoughts down into his heart, the center of the person, as the Bible speaks of it. There he prayed, again and again, the short prayer that the desert fathers had handed down, in the form most often used: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.”

Sometimes nothing seemed to happen. Then the monk simply waited, as the prophet had written long before: “It is good to wait in silence for the LORD’s salvation.”

Who they were

In Volume 4 we followed the Jesus Prayer from the blind man on the road to Jericho into the deserts of Egypt and the monasteries of Gaza and Sinai, and we promised that we would meet the monks of Mount Athos. Here they are.

One of the teachers who brought this way of prayer to Athos was another Gregory, called Gregory of Sinai. He was born near Smyrna, in what is now Turkey, around the 1260s. As a young man he was captured by Turkish raiders. After he was set free, he became a monk at the monastery of Saint Catherine at the foot of Mount Sinai. On the island of Crete he learned the prayer of stillness from an old monk named Arsenios. In the early 1300s he came to Athos and taught it to many. His disciple Kallistos, who later became patriarch of Constantinople, wrote his life.

Gregory of Sinai was careful and wise. In the short writings on prayer that his disciples kept, he warns against chasing after visions or picturing things in the imagination while praying, because such things can deceive us. The heart should simply call on Jesus with humility and wait. He was also gentle with tired beginners: they might pray part of the short prayer, he said, but they should not keep changing its words.

These were not peaceful times. The Byzantine Empire, heir of the old Roman Empire in the east, was growing weak. Turkish pirates raided the coasts, and Athos was attacked. Gregory of Sinai had to flee north to the mountains of Bulgaria, where he died in 1346. Gregory Palamas and the monks with him moved to the city of Thessalonica for safety. Like the poet of Lamentations, who wrote among the ruins of Jerusalem, they learned to wait for God while war and danger surrounded them.

A debate about prayer

In the 1330s a learned monk named Barlaam, who had come to Constantinople from Calabria in southern Italy, was teaching there. He was a brilliant scholar of philosophy, mathematics and astronomy. When he heard how some monks prayed, he was shocked. Sitting with a bowed head and watching the breath seemed to him like superstition. He mocked the hesychasts as people who thought their souls were in their navels.

Barlaam’s deeper concern was serious. He taught that God is so far above us that no one can know Him directly in this life. When the hesychasts said that in prayer some of them had seen a holy light, the same light that shone from Jesus on the mountain of the Transfiguration, Barlaam said that this could not be God Himself. At best it was something God had made.

The monks of Athos asked Gregory Palamas to answer him. Palamas wrote a long defense of the hesychasts, known as the Triads. He agreed with Barlaam that God’s inner being is beyond all knowing, forever. But, he said, God truly gives Himself to us. Through His grace, His energies, His working, the living God touches us, and not only something that stands between us and Him. When Jesus “was transfigured” before the disciples, “His face shone like the sun, and His clothes turned white as light” (Matthew 17:2). That light, said Palamas, was God’s own glory.

Church councils in Constantinople, in 1341 and again in 1351, agreed with Palamas, and the Orthodox Church honors him as a saint and a great teacher. Barlaam returned to Italy. Christians of other traditions have not all agreed with him on every point. But we can all take his main concern to heart: in prayer we do not only think about a distant God. We meet the living God who comes to us. Palamas became archbishop of Thessalonica in 1347. In 1354 he was captured by the Turks and held for about a year. He died in 1359.

Learning to wait

Lamentations 3 is one of the darkest chapters in the Bible. The writer has seen Jerusalem burned and its people taken away. He feels that God has walled him in and shut out his prayer. And then, in the middle of the darkness, he remembers: “It is by the LORD’s loyal love that we have not been wiped out, for His mercies have not failed. They are new each morning” (Lamentations 3:22-23). So he decides to wait, quietly, for God to save.

Andrew Murray, whom we heard in chapter 9, wrote a whole book on waiting for God. On this verse he wrote:

“The quietness is the confession of our impotence, that with all our willing and running, with all our thinking and praying, it will not be done: we must receive it from God.”

Andrew Murray, Waiting on God

“Impotence” means helplessness. Stillness before God says, “Lord, I cannot do this. You must.” Murray gave very practical advice:

“Take time to be separate from all friends and all duties, all cares and all joys; time to be still and quiet before God.”

Andrew Murray, Waiting on God

Three key insights

  1. Stillness before God is not empty but full of His presence. The hesychasts did not seek quiet for its own sake. They sought it in order to be with Jesus, calling on His name.
  2. Waiting in silence is a confession that only God can save. When we stop talking and wait, we admit that we are helpless and that He is good. That is humility and faith together.
  3. In prayer we meet the living God Himself. God’s being is far beyond us, but He truly comes to us by His grace. Prayer is not talking to an empty sky.

For us today

Our world is loud. Phones buzz all day, and music and screens fill every hour. Many believers have never sat in silence before God for even five minutes. The hesychasts remind us that God often speaks, as He did to Elijah, in “a faint sound, thin as silence” (1 Kings 19:12).

They also speak to those who live in hard times. A Christian in a country at war, a family waiting for news of a missing son, a believer in prison for Christ, a farmer waiting for rain that does not come: each of them knows what it is to wait. Lamentations does not tell them to pretend all is well. It tells them that the Lord is good, and that it is good to wait for Him.

And they warn us against two mistakes. One is to think that a technique of breathing or sitting can make God come. It cannot. Gregory of Sinai said the heart must call on Jesus with humility. The other mistake is to despise simple ways of prayer because they look strange. Breathing slowly and praying a short prayer is something any believer can do.

Try this

This week, practice waiting in stillness.

  • Find a quiet seat. Sit somewhere quiet for ten minutes, early in the morning or late at night. Put your phone away.
  • Let your body grow still. Bow your head. Let your breathing become slow and calm.
  • Call on Jesus. Pray gently, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,” perhaps the first half as you breathe in and the second half as you breathe out. When your mind wanders, come back to His name.
  • Wait. After a while, stop speaking. Simply wait in silence before God. Then read Lamentations 3:22-26 and thank Him that His mercies are new this morning.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You are good to all who wait for You and seek You. My life is full of noise, and my heart is full of worries. Teach me to be still before You. When I cannot fix what is broken, help me to wait in silence for Your salvation. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Come to me by Your grace, and let me know that You are near. Thank You that Your mercies have not failed, and that they are new each morning. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • When was the last time you were completely quiet before God? What made it easy or hard?
  • Why do you think the writer of Lamentations could say “it is good” to wait, even in the middle of disaster?
  • How can a short prayer and slow breathing help you to pray? What are its dangers?

fields.title: “All Shall Be Well”
fields.body_html:
“We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good. They are the ones called in keeping with His purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

In May 1373, in the English city of Norwich, a woman lay dying. She was thirty and a half years old. For three days and three nights she had been very ill. On the fourth night she received the last rites of the church, and no one expected her to live until morning. She held on for two more days and nights. On the third night, everyone around her was sure that the end had come.

She was not afraid of death, she tells us, but she was sorry to die young, because she had wanted to live longer to love God better.

Her priest was sent for. When he came, she could no longer speak, and her eyes were fixed upward. He held a cross before her face and said:

“I have brought thee the Image of thy Maker and Saviour: look thereupon and comfort thee therewith.”

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

She turned her eyes to the cross. The room grew dark around her, as if it were night, except for a light on the image of Christ. Her body had gone dead from the middle downward, then the upper part began to die too, and she could hardly breathe. Then suddenly all her pain was taken away, and she felt as well as she had ever been.

Over the next hours she received what she called sixteen “Shewings,” or showings: things that she believed God showed her about His love, mostly as she looked at the cross. In one of them she saw something very small:

“Also in this He shewed me a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball.”

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

She wondered what it could be, and she understood the answer: “it is all that is made.” It was so small that she wondered how it did not simply fall to nothing. And she was answered: “It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it.” God made it, God loves it, and God keeps it.

She recovered, and lived for more than forty years, praying and thinking about what she had seen. We call her Julian of Norwich.

Who she was

We do not even know her real name. Later in life she lived as an anchoress at the church of Saint Julian in Norwich, and she is probably called after that church. An anchoress (or, for a man, an anchorite) was a person who chose to live shut away for life in a small room built against the wall of a church. Usually a bishop blessed the anchoress as she went in, and she did not come out again. One small window looked into the church, so that she could follow the services. Another window opened to the street, and people came to it to ask for prayer and advice. Servants brought food and cared for her needs.

We know she was still there in the early 1400s, because people left her small gifts of money in their wills. A woman named Margery Kempe tells in her own book that she went to Norwich to ask the anchoress Julian for counsel, and that Julian spoke to her kindly about God’s work in the soul.

Julian lived in the hard times we described in chapter 11. The Black Death reached Norwich when she was a small child, and in 1381, when the peasants rose up, there was fighting near the city. Many people wondered whether God had turned against them.

Julian wrote down her showings twice: a short account soon after her illness, and a much longer one many years later, after long reflection. Her writings are the earliest books in English that we know were written by a woman. The Ochorus library has the longer version, Revelations of Divine Love, in the 1901 English of Grace Warrack.

All shall be well

One question troubled Julian deeply. If God is so good, why did He allow sin, which has caused so much pain in the world? It seemed to her that if sin had never begun, all would have been well. Jesus, she says, answered her:

“It behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.”

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

“It behoved” means “it was fitting” or “it had to be.” Julian did not claim to understand this. She said there is a great secret hidden in God that we will see only in heaven. Meanwhile, she was to hold to the faith of the church, and to trust that God would one day make all things well, in a way no one can yet imagine.

Notice that “all shall be well” is not a cheerful saying that pretends pain is not real. Julian saw Christ’s suffering on the cross in great detail. She knew the plague and the sorrows of her city. Near the end of her book she writes that God did not promise that we would never be troubled or afflicted. He said, “Thou shalt not be overcome.”

Paul says something like this in Romans 8. He does not say that all things are good. He says that “for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good” (Romans 8:28). The Puritan pastor Thomas Watson, who wrote a whole book on this verse, put it with a picture from his own day:

“Or as in a watch, the wheels seem to move contrary one to another, but all carry on the motions of the watch: so things that seem to move cross to the godly, yet by the wonderful providence of God work for their good.”

Thomas Watson, All Things for Good

How she prayed

Julian’s book is full of teaching on prayer. She knew how it feels to pray and feel nothing. She says that we often feel “as barren and dry” after our prayers as before. Then she tells what she heard the Lord say:

“Pray inwardly, though thee thinketh it savour thee not: for it is profitable, though thou feel not, though thou see nought; yea, though thou think thou canst not.”

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

To “savour” is to taste. Even when prayer seems to have no taste at all, it pleases God. Julian also heard the Lord say, “I am Ground of thy beseeching.” Our praying begins with God: He wants to give, so He moves us to ask.

For years Julian wondered what all her showings meant. More than fifteen years later, she says, she was answered in her spirit: “Love was His meaning.” Who showed it to her? Love. What did He show her? Love. Why? For love.

Three key insights

  1. God holds all things, even the smallest, because He loves them. The little hazelnut lasted because God loved it. You are held in the same love.
  2. God does not promise we will never suffer, but He promises we will not be overcome. All shall be well is a promise about the end, given to people in the middle of pain. In Christ, nothing is wasted.
  3. We should keep praying even when prayer feels dry, because God delights in it. Our feelings are not the measure of our prayers. God is the ground of our asking, and He receives our prayers with joy.

For us today

Many readers of this book are living in hard places. A family in Haiti rebuilding after a storm, a widow in South Sudan, a young Christian in Iran who has lost his job for his faith, a mother in a hospital ward in Bangladesh: each of them may wonder, as Julian did, how anything can ever be well again. Julian does not offer easy answers. She points to the cross, and to a love that made everything and will not let it go.

Julian’s window also teaches us something. People brought their fears to her, and she pointed them to the love of God. A word of hope from someone who has suffered and still trusts God can carry great weight.

And she gives us words for dark days: all shall be well.

Try this

This week, rest in God’s love with Julian.

  • Hold something small. Hold a small seed, nut or stone in your palm. Thank God that He made it, He loves it, and He keeps it, and that He does the same for you.
  • Pray when it feels dry. Set a time to pray each day this week, and keep it even if you feel nothing. Tell God, “I am praying because You delight in it.”
  • Say Julian’s words. When something worries you, pray, “Lord, all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well, because You love me.”
  • Visit a window. Like Julian, be available to someone who needs to talk. Listen, and pray with them.

A closing prayer

Loving God, You made all things, You love them, and You keep them. Thank You that I am held in Your hand, even when I feel small and weak. Thank You that in Christ You work all things together for good for those who love You. I do not understand all Your ways, but I trust Your love. When I am troubled, do not let me be overcome. When my prayers feel dry, teach me to keep praying. Make all things well, Lord, in Your time, and let me learn that love was Your meaning. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Julian saw the whole world as small as a hazelnut, kept by God’s love. How does that picture make you feel about your own life?
  • What is the difference between “all things are good” and “all things work together for good”?
  • Have you ever kept praying when prayer felt dry? What helped you?

fields.title: Giving God No Rest
fields.body_html:
“I have stationed guards on your walls, Jerusalem; through the whole day and the whole night they will keep calling out, never silent. You who keep reminding the LORD, do not rest, and do not let Him rest either, until He has made Jerusalem secure and made her a city the whole earth praises.” (Isaiah 62:6-7)

Around the year 1375, in Siena, a hill city in the middle of Italy, a young man sat in prison, waiting to die. Later writers give his name as Niccolò di Toldo, from Perugia, and say that he had been condemned for speaking against the rulers of Siena, and that he was filled with fear and anger.

Then a young woman came to visit him. She was the daughter of a man who dyed wool for a living. Her name was Catherine.

Catherine herself tells what happened next, in a letter to her confessor, Raymond of Capua. She prayed with Niccolò, and slowly his fear melted. He made his confession, and on the morning of his death he received Holy Communion, which, Catherine says, he had never received before. Only one fear was left: that he would not be strong at the end. He made her promise to be with him when the time came. “Stay with me, and do not abandon me,” he said. “So it shall not be otherwise than well with me. And I die content.”

Catherine kept her promise. She went ahead to the place of execution and waited there, as she writes, “with constant prayer.” When Niccolò arrived, he was calm. He saw her and smiled. He asked her to make the sign of the cross over him. As he knelt down, she reminded him of the blood of Christ, the Lamb of God, poured out for him. His last words, she says, were the names “Jesus” and “Catherine.” Then he was put to death.

Catherine did not turn away. She believed that she saw, with the eyes of her heart, Christ receiving his soul in mercy. A frightened, angry young man had died in peace, beside a woman who had prayed for him and would not leave him.

Catherine was then about twenty-eight. In the five years she had left, she prayed with a strength that moved popes and cities, and she refused to stop asking God for mercy on His people.

Who she was

Catherine Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, one of the youngest of more than twenty children. The next year the Black Death, which we met in chapter 11, reached Siena. She grew up in a world of fear, sickness and war.

From childhood she wanted to give her life to God. Her family wanted her to marry, but in the end she joined the Mantellate, women in the wider Dominican family who wore a black and white habit but lived in their own homes. For about three years Catherine stayed almost always in a small room in her parents’ house, praying and keeping silence. Then she believed that God was sending her out to serve her neighbors.

She nursed the sick in the hospitals of Siena, and when the plague came back in 1374 she cared for the dying. She visited prisoners.

Catherine learned to read only as an adult, and she wrote mostly by speaking to friends who wrote down her words. Nearly four hundred of her letters survive, to poor women and soldiers, to kings and queens, and to the pope himself. She died in Rome on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three.

The pope in Avignon

Since 1309 the popes had lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in the south of France. Many Christians grieved over this, because Rome was the city of Peter and Paul, and they felt that its bishop should be with his people.

Catherine honored the pope as Christ’s representative on earth. She even called him, in her letters, “sweet Christ on earth.” But she did not flatter him. She wrote to Pope Gregory XI again and again, urging him to return to Rome and to reform the church. “Come, come, come,” she wrote, “and do not wait for time, since time does not wait for you.”

In 1376 she traveled to Avignon herself and met him. His advisers were frightening him with warnings that he would die if he went to Rome. So she wrote to him again: “Up, father, like a man! For I tell you that you have no need to fear.” Later that year Gregory left Avignon, and in January 1377 he entered Rome. Historians agree that many things moved him, and Catherine was only one voice among several. But notice what came before her bold words. In that same letter she told him, “I have prayed, and shall pray, sweet and good Jesus that He free you from all servile fear.” Her letters to the pope grew out of her prayers for him.

How she prayed

Toward the end of her life, Catherine’s friends wrote down a long book that came from her prayer. We call it The Dialogue, because in it a soul speaks with God and God answers. It begins with four requests the soul brought to God: for herself, for the reform of the church, for the whole world, and for a particular need. That is the shape of Catherine’s prayer. She started with her own heart, but she never stopped there.

Again and again in the Dialogue she pleads for the world and the church, like Moses pleading for Israel. She will not let go:

“I pray Your divine and eternal love to take Your revenge on me, and to do mercy to Your people, and never will I depart from before Your presence until I see that you grant them mercy.”

Catherine of Siena, The Dialogue

Notice two things. First, she blames herself before anyone else. She stood with the people she prayed for, not above them. Second, she refuses to leave God’s presence until He shows mercy. That is exactly what Isaiah describes.

Isaiah pictures guards on the walls of Jerusalem who watch and call out day and night. Then God says something surprising to those who pray: keep reminding Him of His promises, and give Him no rest until He has done what He said. God is not tired or forgetful. But He invites His people to pray like this, with holy stubbornness. Jesus taught the same thing when He told a parable “about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

E. M. Bounds wrote about these watchmen:

“The idea is, that these praying ones are those who are the Lord’s remembrancers, those who remind Him of what He has promised, and who give Him no rest till God’s Church is established in the earth.”

E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer

Catherine prayed that way to the very end. A friend who was at her deathbed, Barduccio Canigiani, wrote that as she was dying she prayed especially for the church, for which, she said, she was giving her life. Her last words were the words of Jesus on the cross: “Father, into Your Hands I commend my soul and my spirit.”

Three key insights

  1. God invites His people to pray with holy stubbornness, giving Him no rest until He acts. Isaiah’s watchmen keep calling out day and night. Catherine told God she would not leave His presence until He showed mercy. This is faith that takes God at His word.
  2. Real prayer for others always leads us to stand beside them. Catherine prayed for Niccolò, and then she went to him and stayed with him to the end.
  3. We can speak the truth boldly to leaders when we have first prayed for them humbly. Catherine wrote strong words to the pope, but she prayed for him first, and she counted herself a sinner among sinners.

For us today

Catherine lived with plague, war, cities divided by hatred, and a church that needed renewal. You may live where sickness has emptied homes, or where leaders in the church have failed their people. Catherine shows that such times are not a reason to stop praying. They are a call to keep on until God acts.

She also reminds us that prayer is not only for those with education or power. She was a dyer’s daughter who learned to read late in life, yet God used her prayers to touch prisoners and popes. A widow in a village in Ghana, a factory worker in Vietnam, a student in Peru: any believer can stand as a watchman on the wall.

And prayer must send us out. The people we pray for may be in a hospital ward, a prison cell or the house next door. Sometimes God answers our prayer by sending us to them.

Try this

This week, take your place as a watchman on the wall.

  • Pray Catherine’s four requests. Each day pray for your own heart, for the renewal of the church, for the whole world and for one particular need.
  • Choose one thing and do not let go. Pick one need, perhaps a person far from God, a broken family or your nation, and pray for it every day this week. Remind God of His promises in Scripture.
  • Visit someone who is suffering. Go to someone sick, in prison or alone, and pray with them. Stay with them for a while.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You set watchmen on the walls of Your city and told them not to be silent. Thank You for Your servant Catherine, who would not leave Your presence until You showed mercy, and who stayed beside the dying and the condemned. Make me a watchman too. Give me a heart that keeps reminding You of Your promises, day and night, until You make Your people a joy to the whole earth. Have mercy on Your church and on the world. Free our leaders from fear. And when I pray for those who suffer, send me to stand beside them. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Catherine told God she would not leave His presence until He showed mercy. Is there a need you have stopped praying for? What would it mean to keep reminding God about it?
  • Catherine prayed for Niccolò and then stayed with him to the end. Who might God be asking you not only to pray for, but also to be with?
  • How can we speak the truth to leaders in a way that comes from prayer and love, and not from anger?

  • E. M. Bounds, The Essentials of Prayer, especially “Prayer and Missions”

fields.title: Open My Eyes to Your Word
fields.body_html:
“Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction.” (Psalm 119:18)

In the 1370s and 1380s, if you went to church in an English village, you would hear the Bible read in Latin. Most of the people did not. They knew the stories from sermons and from the paintings on the church walls. But very few had ever held the Scriptures in their own tongue.

At Oxford, England’s great university, a scholar named John Wycliffe became convinced that this had to change. He believed that the Bible is the highest authority for every Christian, and that every Christian should be able to know it.

So in the years around 1380, a group of scholars began to do something new. Working from the Latin Bible that the church had used for a thousand years, they translated the whole of Scripture into English, book by book.

One old manuscript of this first translation has a small note in the middle of the book of Baruch, where the handwriting changes. It says that here the translation of “N” ends, and the translation of “J and others” begins. “N” was probably Nicholas Hereford, one of Wycliffe’s Oxford followers. How much of it Wycliffe translated himself, scholars cannot say; perhaps very little. But he was the one who inspired it. A second, smoother version was finished by his followers in the 1390s, some years after his death.

In that later version, the verse at the head of this chapter reads like this: “Liytne thou myn iyen; and Y schal biholde the merueils of thi lawe.” In modern spelling, that is roughly: Lighten Thou my eyes, and I shall behold the marvels of Thy law. For the first time, an English farmer or weaver could pray those words in his own language, and then open the book and ask God to show him its wonders.

Who he was

John Wycliffe was born in Yorkshire, in the north of England, around 1330. He spent most of his life at Oxford, where he was master of Balliol College and a famous teacher of theology. For a time he served the king of England, and he became well known for his sharp attacks on the wealth and worldly power of the church of his day.

As the years went on, his teaching grew more radical. He argued that the Bible stands above every church leader, including the pope. He also rejected the church’s teaching about how Christ is present in the bread of the Lord’s Supper. That brought him into deep trouble. In 1382 a council of church leaders in London condemned many of his teachings, and some of his friends at Oxford were forced to take back their words. Wycliffe withdrew to Lutterworth, a small town where he was the parish priest. A stroke left him partly paralyzed. Late in 1384 a second stroke struck him while he was at worship in his church, and he died a few days later, on the last day of the year.

We should be fair. Wycliffe could be harsh, and Christians still disagree about some of his ideas. Many of those who opposed him were sincere, and feared that his ideas would bring disorder to church and nation. And many English people who were never his followers owned copies of the English Bible, including nobles, priests and even kings. The translation itself was faithful to the Latin text.

The Lollards

Wycliffe’s followers were given a nickname: Lollards. It probably came from an old Dutch word for someone who mumbles, perhaps mocking the way they murmured prayers and Scripture to themselves.

Most were ordinary people: weavers, tailors, farmers, women and men. They met quietly in each other’s homes, often at night. One would read aloud from a precious handwritten copy of a Gospel or a letter of Paul, and the others listened. Many learned long passages by heart, because books were rare and costly. They learned the Lord’s Prayer, the Ten Commandments and the Creed in English, and they taught them to their children. They prayed in their own language, to a God they believed was listening.

This became dangerous. In 1401 a priest named William Sawtrey became the first Lollard to be burned, and a new law that year allowed people judged to be heretics to be burned. In 1409 the Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Arundel, forbade anyone to make or read a new English translation without a bishop’s permission. For more than a century after that, many Lollards were questioned, made to give up their beliefs in public, or imprisoned. Some were burned. Bishops’ records from the early 1500s still list people accused of owning English Scriptures, or of teaching their families the Lord’s Prayer in English.

John Foxe, the English Protestant who wrote his famous Book of Martyrs in 1563, tells these stories with great feeling. He was writing for one side of a bitter quarrel, and he is not always accurate. For example, he says Wycliffe made the translation himself. But he rightly says that the efforts to stop the English Bible only made people want it more. Those who could not buy a whole copy, he says, got copies of single Gospels or letters. Even Wycliffe’s grave was not left in peace. In 1415 a great church council condemned him, and in 1428 his bones were dug up, burned, and the ashes thrown into the little River Swift at Lutterworth. Foxe wrote:

“But these and all others must know that, as there is no counsel against the Lord, so there is no keeping down of verity, but it will spring up and come out of dust and ashes, as appeared right well in this man; for though they dug up his body, burned his bones, and drowned his ashes, yet the Word of God and the truth of his doctrine, with the fruit and success thereof, they could not burn.”

John Foxe, Fox’s Book of Martyrs

(“Verity” is an old word for truth.)

Take the veil from my eyes

Psalm 119 is the longest psalm in the Bible, and almost every verse speaks of God’s word. Yet the psalmist knows that having the word is not enough. He prays, “Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction” (Psalm 119:18). A veil is a cloth that covers the face. A person can stare at a page and see nothing, because something covers the eyes of the heart. Only God can take that veil away.

This is why the Lollards did not only read. They prayed. They knew that a Bible in English was a great gift, but that God Himself must open their understanding. R. A. Torrey put it simply:

“The author, the Holy Spirit, is right at hand to interpret. To understand the book we must look to Him and the darkest places become clear.”

R. A. Torrey, What the Bible Teaches

The psalmist expects to find wonders, and the Lollards, reading by candlelight in a weaver’s cottage, often did. The same psalm says, “Your word is a lamp to guide my feet and a light for the road I travel” (Psalm 119:105). In the Wycliffite Bible it reads: “Thi word is a lanterne to my feet; and liyt to my pathis.”

Three key insights

  1. Having God’s word is not enough; we need Him to open our eyes to it. The psalmist had God’s word, yet he still prayed for sight. Reading Scripture and praying belong together, because the Spirit who gave the word helps us to understand it.
  2. Believers who gather to read and pray together can keep faith alive in the hardest times. The Lollards had no buildings, no protection and few books. In small groups in their homes they listened to God’s word, learned it by heart and prayed, and their faith lasted for more than a hundred years.
  3. Fire can destroy books and bodies, but it cannot destroy the word of God. Wycliffe’s ashes were thrown into a river, and Lollards suffered and died. But the English Bible was copied again and again, and the word they loved went on.

For us today

Most readers of this book can hold the Bible in their own language. It came to us through the costly work of translators, many of whom suffered for it. In some places believers still meet in secret to read the Scriptures, as the Lollards did. In others, Christians still wait for the Bible in their mother tongue. Thousands of languages in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and the Americas have only part of the Bible, or none at all.

Yet many of us hardly open the Bible we own, or read it without praying. Let the Lollards teach us to read it hungrily, and to ask God each time to open our eyes.

Try this

This week, read and pray like a Lollard.

  • Pray before you read. Each time you open your Bible, pray Psalm 119:18 first: “Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction.”
  • Learn a passage by heart. Choose a short passage, such as Psalm 23 or Matthew 6:9-13, and learn it this week, a few lines a day.
  • Read aloud with others. Gather your family or a few friends. Let one person read a chapter aloud slowly, then pray together about what you heard.
  • Pray for Bible translators. Pray for people still waiting for the Bible in their own language, and for the translators who serve them.

A closing prayer

Lord God, thank You for giving us Your word, and for the men and women who gave their lives so that ordinary people could read it in their own language. Thank You for John Wycliffe and his friends, and for the Lollards who read Your word by candlelight and prayed in their own tongue. Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction. Make Your word a lamp to my feet. Give me a hunger to read it and courage to obey it. Protect those who read it in secret today, and send Your word to every people still waiting for it. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • The Lollards risked their lives to read the Bible in their own language. How does their story make you feel about the Bible you own?
  • Why do you think the psalmist prayed for open eyes, even though he already had God’s word?
  • Who could you read and pray the Scriptures with, the way the Lollards did in their homes?

Read more on Ochorus
