  • John Foxe, Foxe’s Book of Martyrs (For Teens), especially “The Morning Star”
  • R. A. Torrey, What the Bible Teaches, especially “The Work of the Holy Spirit”

fields.title: Praying for Those Who Burn You
fields.body_html:
“But I tell you: love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you, so that you will be children of your Father in heaven. He makes His sun rise on evil people and good people alike, and He sends rain on those who do right and those who do wrong.” (Matthew 5:44-45)

On the morning of 6 July 1415, in the great cathedral of Constance, a city on a lake in southern Germany, a pale, thin man stood before the most important church council of his age. Bishops, cardinals and princes filled the church. Sigismund, the German king who later became emperor, was there. The man was Jan Hus, a preacher from Prague. He had been in prison for more than seven months, sometimes in chains.

Two sentences were read out. The first ordered all his books to be burned. The second declared him a heretic, to be handed over to the city’s rulers for punishment. He would be burned to death that same day.

A friend of Hus was there, a young Czech nobleman’s secretary named Peter of Mladoňovice. He wrote down what happened next. Hus knelt down, and in a loud voice he prayed:

“Lord Jesus Christ, forgive all my enemies, I entreat you, because of your great mercifulness. You know that they have falsely accused me, brought forth false witnesses against me, devised false articles against me. Forgive them because of your immense mercifulness.”

Peter says that many in the council, especially the leading churchmen, mocked him.

Then came a ceremony of shame. They dressed Hus in a priest’s robes and took them off again, piece by piece, to show that he was no longer a priest. They put a tall paper hat on his head, painted with devils. “We commit thy soul to the devil,” the bishops said. Hus answered: “And I commit it to the most sacred Lord Jesus Christ.”

Soldiers led him out of the city to a field among gardens. There, Peter writes, he knelt again, stretched out his arms, lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed the psalms aloud, especially “Have mercy on me, oh God,” and “In thee, oh Lord, do I put my trust.” Some ordinary people standing nearby said, “We know not what he has formerly said or done, but we now see and hear that he prays, and speaks holy words!”

When the fire was lit, Hus began to sing: “Christ, son of the living God, have mercy on us.” He sang it twice. As he began a third time, the wind blew the flames into his face. Still moving his lips in silent prayer, he died.

Who he was

Jan Hus was born around 1370 in Husinec, a small village in southern Bohemia, the land that is now the Czech Republic. He studied at the University of Prague, became a priest and teacher there, and for a time was head of the university.

In 1402 he became the preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague. This large, plain building had been built for one purpose: preaching in Czech, the language of the people. Crowds of ordinary people, rich and poor, came to hear him. He preached against sin in every class of society, including the clergy. He also taught them to sing hymns in their own language.

Hus read the writings of John Wycliffe, whom we met in the last chapter, and agreed with many of his ideas. Like Wycliffe, he said that Christ, not any human leader, is the true head of the church, and that Scripture must judge the church. He spoke out against the selling of indulgences, which were promises that the punishment for sins would be lessened, in exchange for money. This brought him into conflict with the archbishop and the pope. He was excommunicated, or cut off from the church, and in 1412 he left Prague and preached in the countryside, often in the open air.

In 1414 he was called to the Council of Constance. The council had been gathered to heal a great split in the church, when three different men all claimed to be pope. Sigismund promised Hus safe travel, and Hus went, hoping to explain his beliefs. But within a few weeks he was arrested. The council demanded that he take back his teachings. He said he would gladly do so if anyone could show him from Scripture that he was wrong, but he would not swear to deny teachings he said he had never held. And so he was condemned.

We should tell this fairly. The men at Constance believed they were protecting the church from dangerous error, and some of them tried hard to persuade Hus to save his life. The burning of heretics was, sadly, accepted across much of Europe at that time. In 1999, Pope John Paul II spoke of his “deep regret” for the cruel death of Jan Hus.

Praying for his enemies

Hus’s prayer in the cathedral was not a sudden act. In prison he had already been learning to love his enemies. One of his fiercest accusers was a man called Michael de Causis. Hus wrote that Michael came to the prison with men from the council and said to the guards, “By God’s grace we shall soon burn this heretic who has cost me many a florin.” Then Hus added: “Understand that in writing this I do not yearn for vengeance on him; this I have left with God. I am praying for him with all my heart.” In a letter to the people of Bohemia, written four weeks before his death, he spoke of fellow Czechs who had become his fiercest enemies, and he asked his friends: “pray for them, I beseech you.”

This is exactly what Jesus commanded: “love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Jesus did it Himself on the cross: “Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Stephen did it as the stones fell on him: “Lord, do not charge them with this sin” (Acts 7:60).

John Foxe, whom we met in the last chapter, tells how Hus met the paper crown of devils. Foxe is not always exact, but the spirit of his account matches Peter’s:

“My Lord Jesus Christ, for my sake, did wear a crown of thorns; why should not I then, for His sake, again wear this light crown, be it ever so ignominious? Truly I will do it, and that willingly.”

John Foxe, Fox’s Book of Martyrs

(“Ignominious” means shameful.)

Foxe also tells a famous story. “Hus” means “goose” in Czech, and Hus is supposed to have said that they were roasting a goose, but that a swan would come after him, a bird they could neither roast nor boil. Many later saw this as a prophecy of Martin Luther. But this saying is a later tradition. The eyewitness, Peter, does not record it.

Why pray for enemies? For their sake, because God may change their hearts. But also for ours. William Law, the English writer, saw that we cannot keep praying for someone and keep despising them:

“For you cannot possibly despise and ridicule that man, whom your private prayers recommend to the love and favour of God.”

William Law, A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life

Three key insights

  1. Praying for those who hurt us shows that we are children of our Father in heaven. Jesus said that God sends sun and rain on good and evil people alike. When we pray for our enemies, we become like Him.
  2. We can hold firmly to the truth and still pray in love for those who oppose us. Hus would not deny what he believed, even to save his life. But he did not hate his accusers. He prayed for them.
  3. Blessing our enemies in prayer frees our own hearts from bitterness. When we ask God each day to bless those who wronged us, He slowly softens our hearts toward them.

For us today

Many believers today know what it is to be falsely accused, put in prison or threatened because of their faith. In parts of the Middle East, Africa and Asia, Christians face hatred from neighbors and from governments. He shows that it is possible to suffer injustice without letting bitterness take over the heart.

Most of us will never face a fire. But all of us have people who have hurt us: a relative who cheated us, a coworker who lied about us, a neighbor who mocks our faith. Jesus’ command is the same for us. Pray for them. Not only “Lord, stop them,” but “Lord, forgive them and bless them.”

And Hus’s story tells us something about the church. His followers in Bohemia never forgot him. Some of them later formed the Unity of the Brethren, and from them came the Moravian Church, whose praying people we will meet in Volume 7.

Try this

This week, practice praying for those who have wronged you.

  • Name them before God. Write down the name of one person who has hurt you. Each day, pray for that person by name, asking God to bless them.
  • Pray the words of the cross. When anger rises, pray Jesus’ words quietly: “Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing.”
  • Pray for persecutors. Pray for those who imprison or attack Christians in another land, that God would change their hearts.

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus Christ, You prayed for those who crucified You, and You told us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. Thank You for Your servant Jan Hus, who held to the truth and still prayed for those who condemned him. Forgive me for the anger and bitterness I keep in my heart. Today I pray for those who have hurt me: bless them, have mercy on them, and draw them to Yourself. Strengthen Your people who suffer for Your name in every land. When my hour of trial comes, fill my mouth with prayer and my heart with Your peace. Christ, Son of the living God, have mercy on us. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Hus prayed for his enemies on the day they condemned him to death. What do you think made this possible?
  • Is there someone you find it hard to pray for? What might change in you if you prayed for them every day?
  • How can we stand firm for the truth without becoming bitter toward those who disagree with us?

fields.title: “Speak, for Your Servant Is Listening”
fields.body_html:
“The LORD came and took His stand there, and called as before, ‘Samuel! Samuel!’ Samuel replied, ‘Speak, for Your servant is listening.’” (1 Samuel 3:10)

In 1392 a boy of about twelve set out from Kempen, a small town in the Rhineland of Germany, to go to school in Deventer, a busy trading town in the Netherlands. His father was a craftsman, and his mother kept a school for small children. The family name was Hemerken, which means “little hammer.” But the world would come to know the boy by the name of his hometown: Thomas à Kempis, Thomas from Kempen.

His older brother John had gone ahead of him and joined a community of canons, priests who lived together under a rule, at Windesheim, near Deventer. Many years later Thomas remembered what happened when he arrived. His brother sent him to a priest in Deventer named Florentius Radewijns, whose name was loved by many students. Thomas writes that Florentius “kept me for a while with him in his house, being moved thereto by fatherly affection.” He put the boy in the school, gave him the books he needed, and found him a free room with a devout woman who was kind to many poor students.

Thomas never forgot the men he met in Florentius’s house. “Never before could I recollect to have seen such men,” he wrote, “so devout and fervent were they in the love of God and of their neighbour.” They worked hard copying books by hand. And, he says, “In the hours of labour they had recourse to ejaculatory prayer for their consolation.” That is, while they worked, they lifted short prayers to God.

He remembered one small moment for the rest of his life. One day in the choir of the church at Deventer, Florentius stood behind him to share his book for the singing and put his hands upon the boy’s shoulder. Thomas stood still, he says, “hardly daring to move.”

In 1399, when he was about nineteen, Thomas visited a small new monastery on a hill near the town of Zwolle, called Mount Saint Agnes. His brother John was now its leader. Thomas wrote in the monastery’s chronicle that he went there “glad at heart,” asked to stay, and “was received with mercy.” He stayed for more than seventy years.

Who he was

Thomas grew up in a movement called the Modern Devotion. It began with a preacher named Geert Groote, of Deventer, who died in 1384. Groote called people to a simple, sincere life of following Christ. His followers formed houses of the Brethren of the Common Life. They were men, and in other houses women, who lived together, shared their money, worked with their hands, prayed together and read the Scriptures. They took no monastic vows. Some of Groote’s followers became canons, like the community at Mount Saint Agnes.

Thomas’s life there was quiet. He was received as a canon in 1406 and ordained a priest some years later. He taught the novices, the young men who were preparing to join the community. He copied many books, including a complete Bible for the community’s use, which still survives in Darmstadt, Germany. When he died in 1471, in about the ninety-second year of his life, a fellow canon wrote in the chronicle that Thomas “was wondrous comfortable to the troubled and the tempted.” (“Comfortable” here means comforting.)

For his novices Thomas wrote four little books between about 1418 and 1427. They were copied and passed from hand to hand, usually without his name. Later they were gathered into one book named after the title of its first chapter: The Imitation of Christ. For a time scholars argued about who wrote it, but a copy in Thomas’s own handwriting from 1441 survives, and most scholars agree that it is his. After the Bible, it may be the most widely read Christian book in history. Catholics and Protestants alike have loved it; John Wesley published his own English edition of it in 1735.

Listening to God

The Imitation is not mainly a book about how to pray. It is a book about how to follow Jesus with a humble heart. But it is full of prayer, and its third book is written as a conversation between Christ and the disciple. Again and again the disciple stops talking and listens.

That third book opens with a line from the psalms: “I am listening for what God, the LORD, will say” (Psalm 85:8). Its second chapter turns to the story of Samuel.

Samuel was a boy who served in God’s house at Shiloh under the old priest Eli. The Bible tells us that “the word of the LORD was rare in those days” (1 Samuel 3:1). One night the LORD called Samuel by name. Three times Samuel ran to Eli, thinking the old man had called him. At last Eli understood, and told the boy what to say. When the LORD called again, Samuel answered, “Speak, for Your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:10). Samuel grew up, and the LORD “did not let any of his words fall to the ground” (1 Samuel 3:19).

Thomas makes Samuel’s answer his own prayer. He does not want only to hear human teachers, even great ones like Moses and the prophets. He wants God Himself to speak to his heart:

“Not so, Lord, not so do I pray. Rather with Samuel the prophet I entreat humbly and earnestly: ‘Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth.’”

Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ

Then he explains why. Teachers can only bring the words to our ears. Only God can bring them into our hearts:

“They deliver the message; You lay bare the sense. They place before us mysteries, but You unlock their meaning. They proclaim commandments; You help us to keep them. They point out the way; You give strength for the journey.”

Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ

Notice that the boy Samuel already knew the right posture. He did not come with a list of requests. He came with an open ear. Much of our prayer is talking. Thomas reminds us that prayer is also listening: coming before God quietly, with His word open, and saying, “Speak, Lord.”

How does God speak? Thomas would say first of all through the Holy Scriptures, read slowly and humbly. In the first book of the Imitation he gives this advice about reading the Bible:

“We ought not to ask who is speaking, but mark what is said.”

Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ

He lived as he taught. He copied the Bible word by word, by hand, for years. He wrote so humbly that most early readers did not even know his name. The voice he wanted people to hear was not his own, but God’s.

Three key insights

  1. Prayer is not only speaking to God but also listening for His voice. Samuel’s best prayer was a simple, open “Speak.” When we come to God quietly with His word open, we make room for Him to speak.
  2. We hear God best when we care more about His word than about who brings it. Thomas told his readers to “mark what is said,” not to ask who was speaking, and he did not even put his own name on his books. A humble listener can receive God’s word from any faithful messenger.
  3. Kindness to a young believer can shape a whole life of prayer. Florentius took a poor schoolboy into his home, and Thomas never forgot it. A meal, a book or a kind hand on the shoulder, given to someone young in faith, may bear fruit for seventy years.

For us today

Many of us pray the way we might speak to a busy official: we say what we need quickly and then hurry away. Whether we live in a great city like Lagos or Seoul or in a small village, Thomas invites us to stay a little longer and listen.

You do not need a monastery to do this. Remember the Brethren in Deventer: they worked all day, and while they worked they lifted short prayers to God. A mother cooking, a driver in traffic, a farmer in the field can each say quietly, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:9), and then pay attention.

And Thomas’s story is good news for ordinary people. He was not famous in his lifetime. He never preached to great crowds or wrote to popes. He prayed, copied, taught and comforted those who were troubled. God took that hidden faithfulness and used it far beyond anything Thomas could have imagined.

Thomas died in 1471. Within fifty years, in Germany, an Augustinian monk named Martin Luther would begin to call the whole church back to the Scriptures, and in Volume 6, A Mighty Fortress, we will follow the praying people of the Reformation.

Try this

This week, practice listening in prayer.

  • Listen before you ask. When you begin to pray, say the words Eli taught Samuel, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening,” and then wait quietly for a minute before you ask for anything.
  • Read slowly and stop. Read a short passage, then be silent for two or three minutes. Ask, “Lord, what are You saying to me?” Write down any word or phrase that stays with you.
  • Pray while you work. Like the Brethren in Deventer, lift short prayers to God during your daily tasks.
  • Read a chapter of the Imitation. Read “Truth Speaks Inwardly Without the Sound of Words” on Ochorus, slowly and prayerfully.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You called the boy Samuel by name in the night, and You still speak to Your people today. Thank You for Your servant Thomas, who learned from humble teachers, copied Your word with patient hands, and taught many to follow Your Son. Forgive me for talking so much and listening so little. Quiet the noise in my heart. Speak to me through Your word, and give me the grace to understand it, to love it and to obey it. Make my small and hidden life useful in Your hands. Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • How much of your prayer is speaking, and how much is listening? What could help you listen more?
  • Thomas was helped by a kind teacher who took him into his home. Who has helped you in your walk with God, and how might you help someone younger?
  • Thomas lived a quiet, hidden life, yet God used it greatly. What small, faithful work might God be asking of you?

  • A. W. Tozer, The Pursuit of God, especially “The Speaking Voice”

fields.title: Conclusion: Passing the Torch
fields.body_html:
“Grass dries out and flowers droop, but the word of our God holds firm for all time.” (Isaiah 40:8)

In the 1450s, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg finished printing a Bible. He had found a way to make metal letters that could be set in rows, inked and pressed onto paper, again and again. A book that had taken a monk many months to copy by hand could now be printed many times over in the same time.

For a thousand years, most of the prayers in this book had been written slowly, by hand, by candlelight. Within a few generations of Gutenberg, they could be printed and carried anywhere. The Imitation of Christ was among the most often printed books of all. Soon the Bible itself would be printed in the languages people spoke at home.

The word of God had held firm all through those thousand years, as Isaiah said it would. Kingdoms rose and fell. Plagues came and went. The church grew, and sinned, and was renewed. And in every century, the word of God was read, sung and prayed by people who loved it.

What the witnesses taught us

Here, in a few lines, is some of what the witnesses of this book taught us about prayer:

  • Praise offered seven times a day teaches us that the whole day belongs to God, and ordinary work done for God becomes part of our worship (chapter 1, Benedict).
  • Fasting together, as a whole church, teaches us that we need God more than food (chapter 2, the church of Ethiopia).
  • No prayer offered to God is lost, even when the church that prayed it is forgotten (chapter 3, the Church of the East in China).
  • No part of an ordinary day is too small to bring to God in prayer (chapter 4, Columba and Celtic prayer).
  • Honest confession is the doorway to God’s mercy, not a wall against it (chapter 5, Gregory of Narek).
  • Even the best minds must ask God to teach them how to seek Him (chapter 6, Anselm).
  • Our love for God is always an answer to His love for us (chapter 7, Bernard of Clairvaux).
  • All creation is a choir of praise, and prayer lets us join in (chapter 8, Francis of Assisi).
  • We become like the One we look at (chapter 9, Clare of Assisi).
  • Before we study about God, we should speak to God (chapter 10, Thomas Aquinas).
  • Love can reach God where our thinking cannot (chapter 11, The Cloud of Unknowing).
  • Stillness before God is not empty but full of His presence (chapter 12, the hesychasts of Mount Athos).
  • God does not promise we will never suffer, but He promises we will not be overcome (chapter 13, Julian of Norwich).
  • God invites His people to pray with holy stubbornness, giving Him no rest until He acts (chapter 14, Catherine of Siena).
  • Having God’s word is not enough; we need Him to open our eyes to it (chapter 15, John Wycliffe and the Lollards).
  • Praying for those who hurt us shows that we are children of our Father in heaven (chapter 16, Jan Hus).
  • Prayer is not only speaking to God but also listening for His voice (chapter 17, Thomas à Kempis).

You will find every one of these lessons gathered by theme in Appendix 1, and every Scripture in this book listed in Bible order in Appendix 2.

Seven times a day

The title of this book comes from a verse that Benedict wrote into his Rule for monks: “I praise you seven times every day because your rulings are righteous” (Psalm 119:164).

Few of us will ever live in a monastery, and we are not meant to copy every practice of these believers. But the heart of that verse belongs to all of us. The witnesses in this book did not wait until they felt like praying. They gave prayer a place in the day, and then they kept that place, in good times and in bad. Benedict’s monks stopped their work when the bell rang. Columba blessed the milk pail and the grain, and long after him the people of the Scottish islands prayed as they lit the fire. The monks of Athos prayed with every breath. Julian kept praying even when her prayer felt dry, because God delights in it. Thomas à Kempis, who never became famous in his lifetime, spent some seventy years in one small monastery, praying, copying and teaching, and wrote a book that has helped more people pray than he could have dreamed.

That is the gift of this volume. It shows us that prayer can shape a whole day, a whole life and a whole people, if it is given room and kept faithfully.

The torch is passed

By the year 1500, many in the Western church longed for renewal. Wycliffe and Hus had called the church back to the word of God, and both had been condemned for it. Thomas à Kempis had called believers back to a humble, inward life with Christ. The printing presses were ready.

In Volume 6, A Mighty Fortress, we will see what happened next. We will meet Martin Luther, who is remembered for saying that the busier he was, the more he needed to pray, and who wrote his barber a letter on a simple way to pray. We will kneel with John Calvin, who called prayer “the principal exercise of faith,” and pray in English with Thomas Cranmer’s Book of Common Prayer. We will hear John Knox plead for Scotland. And we will learn that renewal came on both sides of the great divide: Teresa of Ávila taught that prayer is friendship with God, Ignatius of Loyola taught believers to search their hearts before Him, and Francis de Sales taught busy people to pray. We will hide with the secret Christians of Japan, kneel with Lancelot Andrewes at midnight, and end in a monastery kitchen with Brother Lawrence, practicing the presence of God among the pots and pans.

Those believers did not start from nothing. They prayed the same psalms that Benedict’s monks had sung. They read the same Scriptures that Wycliffe’s followers had copied in secret. Many of them treasured The Imitation of Christ. The torch was passed.

Your turn

The witnesses of this book now pass the torch to you.

So give prayer a place in your day, and keep it, as Benedict did. Bring the small tasks of your day to God, as Columba did. When your heart is heavy with sin, cry to God from the depths, and trust His mercy, as Gregory did. Seek God’s face because He has invited you. Love Him because He first loved you. Join creation in praise, even when life is hard. Look long at Christ, until you begin to reflect Him. Ask for wisdom before you study, and let love reach where your thinking cannot. Be still before God and wait for Him. Trust that all shall be well. Pray for the church and the world with holy stubbornness. Ask God to open your eyes before you read His word. Pray for those who hurt you. And every day, before you speak to God, take a moment to listen.

A closing prayer

Lord God, You have been our home through every generation. Thank You for the monks and nuns, the missionaries and teachers, the poets and preachers who kept praying through a thousand years. Thank You for Benedict and Columba, for the church in Ethiopia and the church on the Silk Road, for Anselm and Bernard, Francis and Clare, Julian and Catherine, Wycliffe and Hus and Thomas à Kempis, and for all whose names only You know. Teach me to give You my days, seven times a day and in every hour between. Open my eyes to Your word, and open my ears to Your voice. Make me humble, faithful and full of love, and let my prayers rise with all Your people, from where the sun comes up to where it goes down. Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening. Amen.

fields.title: Appendix 1: Key Insights
fields.body_html:
Every chapter of this book closes with three key insights. Here they are gathered by theme, each pointing back to the chapter where it is taught and to that chapter’s key verse.

The Father’s Love

  • Even the best minds must ask God to teach them how to seek Him. Chapter 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • Our love for God is always an answer to His love for us. Chapter 7, Jesus, the Very Thought of You (1 John 4:19)
  • God holds all things, even the smallest, because He loves them. Chapter 13, “All Shall Be Well” (Romans 8:28)

Learning to Pray

  • The prayers of others can give us words when our own words fail. Chapter 5, Out of the Depths (Psalm 130:1-4)
  • Faith and careful thinking are friends, and both can lead us to prayer. Chapter 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • We become like the One we look at. Chapter 9, Gazing on Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18)
  • One short word of love from the heart can pierce heaven. Chapter 11, A Simple Reaching for God (Psalm 73:25)
  • Having God’s word is not enough; we need Him to open our eyes to it. Chapter 15, Open My Eyes to Your Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • Prayer is not only speaking to God but also listening for His voice. Chapter 17, “Speak, for Your Servant Is Listening” (1 Samuel 3:10)

Making Room for Prayer

  • Praise offered seven times a day teaches us that the whole day belongs to God. Chapter 1, Ora et Labora: Pray and Work (Psalm 119:164)
  • Fasting together, as a whole church, teaches us that we need God more than food. Chapter 2, Ethiopia Stretches Out Her Hands (Psalm 68:31)
  • No part of an ordinary day is too small to bring to God in prayer. Chapter 4, The Prayers of Ordinary Days (Psalm 121:8)
  • To meet God we must sometimes shut the door on our cares for a while. Chapter 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • A hidden life of prayer is never a wasted life. Chapter 9, Gazing on Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18)
  • Before we study about God, we should speak to God. Chapter 10, A Prayer Before Study (James 1:5)
  • Stillness before God is not empty but full of His presence. Chapter 12, Waiting in Stillness (Lamentations 3:25-26)

Asking Boldly

  • God gives wisdom gladly to everyone who asks Him in faith. Chapter 10, A Prayer Before Study (James 1:5)
  • We can speak the truth boldly to leaders when we have first prayed for them humbly. Chapter 14, Giving God No Rest (Isaiah 62:6-7)

Persistence

  • We should keep praying even when prayer feels dry, because God delights in it. Chapter 13, “All Shall Be Well” (Romans 8:28)
  • God invites His people to pray with holy stubbornness, giving Him no rest until He acts. Chapter 14, Giving God No Rest (Isaiah 62:6-7)

Faith

  • God’s promise reached Africa long before many other lands heard the gospel. Chapter 2, Ethiopia Stretches Out Her Hands (Psalm 68:31)
  • No prayer offered to God is lost, even when the church that prayed it is forgotten. Chapter 3, Prayer on the Silk Road (Malachi 1:11)
  • Love can reach God where our thinking cannot. Chapter 11, A Simple Reaching for God (Psalm 73:25)
  • In prayer we meet the living God Himself. Chapter 12, Waiting in Stillness (Lamentations 3:25-26)

Humility and Mercy

  • Honest confession is the doorway to God’s mercy, not a wall against it. Chapter 5, Out of the Depths (Psalm 130:1-4)
  • Even the holiest believers need God’s mercy for their mistakes. Chapter 7, Jesus, the Very Thought of You (1 John 4:19)
  • All our learning is straw beside the glory of God Himself. Chapter 10, A Prayer Before Study (James 1:5)
  • Waiting in silence is a confession that only God can save. Chapter 12, Waiting in Stillness (Lamentations 3:25-26)
  • We hear God best when we care more about His word than about who brings it. Chapter 17, “Speak, for Your Servant Is Listening” (1 Samuel 3:10)

Forgiveness

  • God forgives us so that we will hold Him in awe, not so that we will treat sin as a small thing. Chapter 5, Out of the Depths (Psalm 130:1-4)
  • Praise can become a peacemaker. Chapter 8, Praise for Brother Sun (Psalm 148:3)
  • Blessing our enemies in prayer frees our own hearts from bitterness. Chapter 16, Praying for Those Who Burn You (Matthew 5:44-45)

Thanksgiving

  • All creation is a choir of praise, and prayer lets us join in. Chapter 8, Praise for Brother Sun (Psalm 148:3)

Guidance and Surrender

  • Ordinary work, done for God, becomes part of our worship. Chapter 1, Ora et Labora: Pray and Work (Psalm 119:164)
  • God can use a captive to bring His light to a nation. Chapter 2, Ethiopia Stretches Out Her Hands (Psalm 68:31)
  • The Lord who guards our going out and coming in is with us on every road. Chapter 4, The Prayers of Ordinary Days (Psalm 121:8)
  • Having God Himself is enough, even when we cannot understand His ways. Chapter 11, A Simple Reaching for God (Psalm 73:25)

Prayer in Suffering and Testing

  • The church’s true strength is in prayer and love, not in the favor of the powerful. Chapter 3, Prayer on the Silk Road (Malachi 1:11)
  • Troubles that drive us to God can teach us to love Him for Himself. Chapter 7, Jesus, the Very Thought of You (1 John 4:19)
  • We can thank God for His gifts even when we can no longer enjoy them. Chapter 8, Praise for Brother Sun (Psalm 148:3)
  • God does not promise we will never suffer, but He promises we will not be overcome. Chapter 13, “All Shall Be Well” (Romans 8:28)
  • Fire can destroy books and bodies, but it cannot destroy the word of God. Chapter 15, Open My Eyes to Your Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • We can hold firmly to the truth and still pray in love for those who oppose us. Chapter 16, Praying for Those Who Burn You (Matthew 5:44-45)

Praying Together

  • Praying the Psalms together teaches us to pray with the whole church. Chapter 1, Ora et Labora: Pray and Work (Psalm 119:164)
  • God’s name is great among the nations, and His people pray to Him in every place. Chapter 3, Prayer on the Silk Road (Malachi 1:11)
  • Believers who gather to read and pray together can keep faith alive in the hardest times. Chapter 15, Open My Eyes to Your Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • Kindness to a young believer can shape a whole life of prayer. Chapter 17, “Speak, for Your Servant Is Listening” (1 Samuel 3:10)

Praying for Others

  • A blessing can be our last gift to those we love. Chapter 4, The Prayers of Ordinary Days (Psalm 121:8)
  • Friends who pray for one another can strengthen each other across great distances. Chapter 9, Gazing on Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18)
  • Real prayer for others always leads us to stand beside them. Chapter 14, Giving God No Rest (Isaiah 62:6-7)
  • Praying for those who hurt us shows that we are children of our Father in heaven. Chapter 16, Praying for Those Who Burn You (Matthew 5:44-45)
